Terminology: meningitis, cerebritis, abscess, encephalitisMeningitis = microorganisms and inflammatory cells within the subarachnoid space (SAS). Cerebritis = cerebral purulent parenchymal infection. Encephalitis = parenchymal infection.Cerebral abscess = walled-off infection: abundant PMNLs, necrotic center, surrounded by granulation tissue, dense fibrovascular capsule and a gliotic rim.Meningitis is in the SAS (meninges); cerebritis, abscess and encephalitis are in the parenchyma.Cerebritis is purulent and not walled off. An abscess is walled off (capsule + gliosis).⭐ Meningitis = organisms + inflammatory cells in the subarachnoid space. Abscess = walled-off necrotic PMN focus with capsule and gliotic rim.
Pathology of CNS Infections
p.4
Acute bacterial meningitis (ABM)Bacterial infection of the leptomeninges / SAS. Raised ICP causes altered mental status.Gross: thick layer of suppurative exudate covering the brain surface (convexities and base) + thickening of the leptomeninges. Micro: neutrophilic infiltrate around blood vessels in the Virchow-Robin spaces, which may extend to the cerebral parenchyma.Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness (resists passive forward flexion), Brudzinski sign (hips and knees flex when the neck is flexed), Kernig sign (resists full leg extension with hips flexed), altered mental status from ↑ICP, focal or generalized seizures. CSF: PMNs greatly ↑, protein ↑, glucose <50% of blood glucose (may be extremely low); Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR. MRI T1 + contrast: leptomeningeal enhancement.PMNs + very low glucose in CSF. Pus over the convexities and base, with leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI.⭐ ABM: suppurative exudate over the brain + neutrophils in Virchow-Robin spaces; CSF has PMNs, ↑protein and glucose <50% of blood.

COMPARE: CSF in meningitis (normal vs bacterial vs viral vs TB vs fungal)Lecture CSF table: cell type, protein, glucose and specific tests for each cause.Normal CSF: all lymphocytes (0–5 cells/mcL), protein <40 mg/dL, glucose >50% of blood glucose.Bacterial: PMNs, often greatly ↑; protein ↑; glucose <50% (may be extremely low); Gram stain/culture/PCR. Viral: lymphocytes (PMNs in first 24–48 h); protein ↑; glucose usually normal; PCR (enterovirus, HSV, VZV, West Nile), IgM. TB: mixed PMN + lymphocyte pleocytosis; protein ↑; glucose <50%; acid-fast stain, PCR, mycobacterial culture (≥30 mL), IFN-γ, Xpert MTB/RIF. Fungal: usually lymphocytes; protein ↑; glucose <50%; cryptococcal antigen, India ink (Cryptococcus), Coccidioides/Histoplasma antigen, culture. Abscess: high WBC, ↑protein, glucose normal.Low glucose = bacterial, TB or fungal. Normal glucose = viral (and abscess). PMNs = bacterial. Lymphocytes = viral or fungal. Mixed = TB.⭐ CSF glucose is normal in viral meningitis and low (<50% of blood) in bacterial, TB and fungal; PMNs point to bacterial.

Cerebral (brain) abscessLocalized focus of necrosis of brain tissue with inflammation, usually bacterial. Routes: direct implantation, local extension from adjacent foci, hematogenous. Risk factors: infective endocarditis, congenital heart disease, chronic pulmonary disease, immunosuppression.Layers from inside out: central liquefactive necrosis, then granulation tissue, then a fibrosis layer (fibroblasts + collagen), then outermost gliosis (astrocytes, microglia, edema).Progressive focal neurologic deficits, signs of ↑ICP, herniation. Rupture causes ventriculitis or meningitis. Venous sinus thrombosis. CSF: high WBC, ↑protein, glucose normal. CT + contrast: enhancing capsule, hypodense center and edema. MRI T1: capsule enhances, interior hypointense. MRI T2: edema bright, capsule hypointense.Ring-enhancing capsule around liquefied pus. Unlike meningitis, CSF glucose is normal.⭐ Abscess = liquefactive necrosis + granulation tissue + fibrous capsule + gliosis; ring (capsule) enhancement; CSF glucose normal; risk = endocarditis / congenital heart disease.

COMPARE: cerebral abscess vs cerebral infarctAbscess: infectious necrosis that becomes walled off. Infarct: ischemic necrosis.Abscess (gross): central cavity containing purulent material bounded by a distinct abscess wall (capsule). Infarct: softened, discolored tissue with no capsule or pus-filled cavity.Abscess: enhancing capsule on CT/MRI with fever and infectious risk factors.Look for the wall: a pus-filled cavity with a fibrous capsule = abscess.⭐ An abscess has a pus-filled cavity with a defined fibrous wall; an infarct has no capsule.

CNS tuberculosisMycobacterium tuberculosis: diffuse meningoencephalitis. Chronic TB meningitis causes arachnoid fibrosis, then communicating hydrocephalus. Obliterative endarteritis causes arterial occlusion and brain infarction.Gross: base of the brain: gelatinous or fibrinous exudate. Micro: well-formed granulomas with caseous necrosis and giant cells; obliterative endarteritis with marked intimal thickening.Headache, malaise, mental confusion, vomiting. Complications: communicating hydrocephalus, infarcts. CSF: mixed PMN + lymphocyte pleocytosis, ↑protein, glucose <50%; acid-fast stain, PCR, Xpert MTB/RIF.Basal gelatinous exudate + caseating granulomas, leading to hydrocephalus and infarcts from endarteritis.⭐ TB meningitis = basal gelatinous exudate, caseating granulomas, arachnoid fibrosis causing communicating hydrocephalus, obliterative endarteritis causing infarcts.

Neurosyphilis: meningovascular and paretic (general paresis)Treponema pallidum: manifestation of tertiary syphilis. Meningovascular: meningitis at the base of the brain + obliterative endarteritis, then fibrosis, occlusion and stroke. Paretic: invasion of the brain (usually frontal lobe) by T. pallidum.Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cells and lymphocytes around blood vessels (perivascular round cell infiltrate). Cerebral gummas (plasma cell-rich mass lesions), which may occur in the meninges. Opacified meninges (syphilitic meningitis).Paretic neurosyphilis (general paresis of the insane): cognitive deficits, delusions of grandeur, mood alteration, dementia. Meningovascular: stroke.Plasma-cell perivascular cuffing + gummas. General paresis = frontal-lobe dementia with grandiosity.⭐ Neurosyphilis = tertiary syphilis: obliterative endarteritis with plasma cells, gummas, and general paresis (dementia + delusions of grandeur).

Tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis)Treponema pallidum: damage to the sensory axons in the dorsal roots.Dorsal root / posterior column degeneration (no separate histology slide).Impaired vibration and joint-position sense in feet and legs; positive Romberg sign; loss of pain sensation, causing skin and joint damage (Charcot joints); lancinating pains (sharp, stabbing, brief, mostly in the legs, seen in 90%); absent ankle and leg DTRs; Argyll-Robertson pupil; high-stepping gait.Proprioceptive loss + Romberg + Argyll-Robertson pupil + lightning pains.⭐ Tabes dorsalis = dorsal root sensory loss: Romberg +, Charcot joints, lancinating pains, absent ankle reflexes, Argyll-Robertson pupil.

Toxoplasmosis (cerebral)Toxoplasma gondii. Opportunistic infection in HIV with CD4 <100/μL. Immunocompetent: contact with cat feces, raw beef, handling uncooked mutton. Congenital: maternal parasitemia from a primary (asymptomatic) infection during pregnancy.Multiple cerebral abscesses. Organisms in pseudocystic bradyzoite form and dispersed single tachyzoite form.Congenital: fever, rash, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, chorioretinitis, microcephaly, hydrocephalus, cerebral calcifications, psychomotor retardation. HIV: single seizure, focal neurologic syndrome, headache or other signs of ↑ICP.HIV with CD4 <100 + multiple abscesses with bradyzoite cysts. Congenital triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, calcifications.⭐ Toxoplasma: multiple brain abscesses in AIDS (CD4 <100); congenital chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications.

CryptococcosisCryptococcus neoformans: occurs in both normal and immunocompromised hosts. Lesions involve the meninges, cortical gray matter and basal nuclei. Yeast 5–10 µm with a thick gelatinous polysaccharide capsule.Thickened meninges. Granulomas (fibroblasts, giant cells, organism aggregates, necrosis). Cortical cysts of gelatinous material + many organisms expanding the Virchow-Robin spaces (soap-bubble appearance). Capsule stains intense red with PAS and mucicarmine.CSF India ink: halo around the refractile wall of thick, encapsulated yeasts. CSF (fungal): usually lymphocytes, ↑protein, glucose <50%; cryptococcal antigen test.Soap-bubble cysts in the gray matter + India-ink halo + mucicarmine-red capsule.⭐ Cryptococcus: encapsulated yeast with India ink halo and a mucicarmine-positive capsule; soap-bubble lesions in the Virchow-Robin spaces.

HSV encephalitisAlmost always HSV-1. The most serious and most common viral encephalitis.Inferior and medial temporal lobes and orbital gyri of the frontal lobes: hemorrhagic necrosis (atrophic, hemorrhagic temporal lobe, cortical bleeding). Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in glia and neurons: Cowdry type A.Fever, headache, seizures, confusion, stupor, coma. May be preceded by olfactory or gustatory hallucinations, temporal lobe seizures, personality change, bizarre or psychotic behavior, delirium, aphasia, hemiparesis. MRI T2: temporal lobe hyperintensity (often unilateral).Hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe + Cowdry A inclusions.⭐ HSV-1 encephalitis = hemorrhagic necrosis of the inferior/medial temporal lobes and orbitofrontal gyri; Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions; T2-bright temporal lobe.

CMV encephalitisCMV: CNS involvement in fetuses and immunosuppressed individuals. In the fetus, brain destruction deranges neuronal migration, causing microcephaly.Fetus: periventricular necrosis and calcification. CMV intranuclear inclusions (in large cells).Immunosuppressed: subacute encephalitis. Fetus: microcephaly. CT: chunky periventricular calcifications.Periventricular calcification (compare toxoplasmosis: scattered cerebral calcifications).⭐ Congenital CMV = periventricular necrosis/calcification and microcephaly; intranuclear inclusions.

RabiesRabies virus: transdermal inoculation by an animal bite. Low-income countries: dogs. US: dogs and cats (domestic); raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats (wild).Negri bodies: cytoplasmic, round to oval, eosinophilic, sharply delineated inclusions in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.Prodrome of 2–4 days: fever, headache, malaise. Then apprehension, dysarthria, psychomotor overactivity, dysphagia (salivation, frothing at the mouth), throat spasms when trying to swallow water or even at the sight of water (hydrophobia). Facial numbness, diplopia, facial spasms, seizures, confusion, psychosis, then coma and death.Its inclusion is cytoplasmic (Negri body); the other viral inclusions are intranuclear. Clinical sign: hydrophobia.⭐ Rabies: Negri bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions) in hippocampal pyramidal neurons and Purkinje cells; hydrophobia.

PoliomyelitisPoliovirus: affects the anterior horn motor neurons of the spinal cord.Mononuclear cell perivascular cuffs. Neuronophagia of anterior horn motor neurons. Central chromatolysis.Flaccid paralysis with muscle wasting and hyporeflexia (LMN). Involvement of the diaphragm and intercostals causes respiratory compromise.Pure LMN flaccid paralysis; neuronophagia in the anterior horn.⭐ Polio = anterior horn cell destruction (neuronophagia, central chromatolysis) causing flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia and respiratory failure.

HIV-associated dementia (HIV encephalopathy)HIV, later stages of infection, usually CD4 <200/mm3. Now generally called HIV encephalopathy.Chronic inflammatory reaction. Microglial nodules (clusters of microglia + lymphocytes). Multinucleated giant cells.Slowly or subacutely progressive dementia (can't follow conversations, slow at daily tasks, forgetful). Limb incoordination, gait ataxia. Brisk reflexes, Babinski, grasp and suck reflexes. Leg weakness progressing to paraplegia, bladder and bowel incontinence. Imaging: cerebral atrophy (wide sulci), ventricular enlargement.Microglial nodules + multinucleated giant cells; diffuse atrophy rather than a focal mass.⭐ HIV encephalopathy (CD4 <200): microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells; progressive dementia with atrophy.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)JC polyomavirus infects oligodendrocytes, causing demyelination. Occurs almost exclusively in immunosuppressed patients.Patches of irregular, ill-defined demyelination in the cerebral hemispheres, brainstem and cerebellum. Enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei with glassy amphophilic intranuclear viral inclusions. Bizarre giant astrocytes with 1 to several irregular, hyperchromatic nuclei.Personality change, intellectual impairment; hemiparesis progressing to quadriparesis, visual field defects, cortical blindness, aphasia, ataxia, dysarthria, dementia, confusion, coma. Radiology: non-enhancing demyelinating lesions.White-matter demyelination with no enhancement in an immunosuppressed patient; virus is in the oligodendrocytes.⭐ PML = JC virus in oligodendrocytes: glassy intranuclear inclusions, bizarre astrocytes, non-enhancing multifocal demyelination in immunosuppressed patients.

COMPARE: viral inclusions (HSV vs CMV vs rabies vs PML)Where each virus leaves its inclusion.HSV: eosinophilic intranuclear (Cowdry A) in glia + neurons. CMV: intranuclear CMV inclusions. Rabies: cytoplasmic Negri bodies in hippocampal pyramidal neurons + Purkinje cells. PML: glassy amphophilic intranuclear inclusions in enlarged oligodendrocytes. HIV: no inclusion; microglial nodules + multinucleated giant cells.HSV: temporal lobe. CMV: periventricular. Rabies: hippocampus/cerebellum. PML: white matter.Only rabies has a cytoplasmic inclusion.⭐ The Negri body (rabies) is the cytoplasmic inclusion; HSV (Cowdry A), CMV and JC (oligodendrocyte) inclusions are intranuclear.

Spongiform encephalopathy (prion disease; CJD)Protein misfolding disorder: PrP undergoes a conformational change from the normal α-helix isoform (PrPc) to an abnormal β-pleated sheet isoform (PrPsc), which resists protease digestion and tends to aggregate. Sources: contaminated food, medical instruments (corneal or dural transplants, deep brain electrodes), cadaveric human growth hormone.Spongiform transformation of the cerebral cortex and deep gray matter (caudate, putamen): uneven, small, apparently empty vacuoles of varying sizes in the neuropil and neuronal perikaryon.CJD = the most common prion disease: subtle memory and behavior changes, then a rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus (involuntary jerks on sudden stimulation), ataxia.Rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus; vacuoles with no inflammation.⭐ CJD: PrPc (α-helix) changes to PrPsc (β-pleated, protease resistant), causing spongiform vacuoles in the cortex and caudate/putamen, rapid dementia and startle myoclonus.

NeoplasiaPathology of CNS Tumors [Neoplasia · Pathology]· 13FORMAT: one row per tumor: demographics/genetics/location · gross & histology buzzwords · clinical/prognosis · what sets it apart
DiseaseEtiology · pathogenesis · risk / geneticsGross & micro (buzzwords)Clinical · CSF · imagingKey differentiator⭐ Will Be TestedImage
CNS tumors: general features and histogenesisHistogenesis: neuroectodermal stem cells give rise to: glial progenitors (astrocytes → astrocytomas; oligodendrocytes → oligodendroglioma; ependymocytes → ependymoma, choroid plexus papilloma/carcinoma); neuronal progenitors (neurons → ganglioglioma; neuronal progenitor remnants → medulloblastoma); neural crest (meningeal cells → meningioma; autonomic/DRG neurons + adrenal medulla → neuroblastoma; Schwann cells → schwannoma; melanocytes → melanoma). Characterized by demographics, genetics, location, gross, histopathology and clinical correlates.A mass (space-occupying lesion) seen on MRI. Local growth is invasive: no capsule even in histologically benign tumors, though often well circumscribed. Metastases stay within the CNS (via CSF).Clinical malignancy: even benign tumors cause ↑ICP and herniation, and posterior-fossa tumors directly injure brainstem vital centers. Raised ICP: headache, nausea/vomiting, neurocognitive dysfunction. Focal deficits: seizures, weakness, sensory loss, aphasia.Behaves as malignant because of location, regardless of grade. Spread is within the CNS (CSF).⭐ CNS tumors are 'clinically malignant': no capsule, ↑ICP and herniation even when benign, and metastasis via CSF within the CNS.

COMPARE: CNS tumors in children vs adultsChildren: CNS tumors are common. Adults: rare.Children: mostly infratentorial (more than supratentorial). Adults: supratentorial.Most common in children: pilocytic astrocytoma, glioblastoma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma. Most common in adults: meningioma, glioblastoma, craniopharyngioma (covered in Endo 2), vestibular (CN VIII) schwannoma.Child + posterior fossa = pilocytic / medulloblastoma / ependymoma. Adult + supratentorial = meningioma / GBM.⭐ Children: infratentorial (pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma). Adults: supratentorial (meningioma, GBM).

Astrocytoma WHO classification (2016)Localized, grade I: pilocytic astrocytoma (BRAF fusion/duplication); subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, SEGA (TSC1/2 mutation). Infiltrating: diffuse/fibrillary, grade II (IDH + TP53); anaplastic astrocytoma, grade III (IDH + TP53); secondary glioblastoma, grade IV (IDH + TP53); primary glioblastoma, grade IV (IDH-wildtype + TERT-promoter mutation and/or EGFR/ERBB1).Localized = circumscribed. Infiltrating = diffuse invasive growth. Without genetic testing the label is NOS (not otherwise specified).IDH = isocitrate dehydrogenase. TERT = telomerase reverse transcriptase.IDH-mutant tumors are the diffuse → anaplastic → secondary GBM line; primary GBM is IDH-wildtype.⭐ IDH + TP53 marks the diffuse astrocytoma → anaplastic → secondary GBM line; primary GBM is IDH-wildtype with TERT/EGFR; SEGA = TSC1/2.

Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO I)The most common CNS tumor in children. BRAF fusion/duplication. Location: cerebellar hemispheres and vermis; periaqueductal area, optic nerve, chiasm.Gross: well demarcated, often cystic with a mural nodule. Micro: pilocytic (hair-like) astrocytes; Rosenthal fibers (coarse, elongated intracytoplasmic inclusions).Very good prognosis with surgery. MRI: cerebellar cyst + nodule.Child + cerebellar cyst with mural nodule + Rosenthal fibers.⭐ Pilocytic astrocytoma: child, cerebellum, cyst with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, BRAF; cured by surgery.

Diffuse (fibrillary) astrocytoma (WHO II)Adults. IDH mutation + TP53 mutation. Location: cerebral hemispheres, at the junction of white and gray matter.Gross: white tissue, no capsule. Micro: well-differentiated astrocytes with invasive growth.Mean survival with chemo- and radiotherapy: 6–8 years. Progresses to anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma.Low grade but infiltrative, so it is not curable and progresses to secondary GBM.⭐ Diffuse astrocytoma: adult, IDH + TP53, infiltrative at the gray–white junction; progresses to anaplastic astrocytoma and then secondary GBM.

Glioblastoma (WHO IV)Most common malignant CNS tumor in adults. Secondary (10%): IDH + TP53 mutation. Primary (90%): IDH-wildtype + TERT-promoter mutation and/or ERBB1 (EGFR) overexpression/amplification. Location: cerebral hemisphere white matter.Gross: invasive; necrosis, cysts, hemorrhages; butterfly pattern (crosses the corpus callosum) in advanced cases. Micro: necrosis + hemorrhage, pseudopalisading, highly pleomorphic cells, high mitotic activity, vascular endothelial proliferation, GFAP+.Mean survival: secondary GBM 2–4 years; primary GBM 0.5–2 years. Rarely metastasizes (within the CNS); patients usually die before metastases appear.Pseudopalisading necrosis + endothelial proliferation; butterfly lesion crossing the corpus callosum.⭐ GBM: necrosis with pseudopalisading + microvascular (endothelial) proliferation, GFAP+, butterfly lesion; primary = IDH-wildtype (90%).

COMPARE: rosette typesFlexner-Wintersteiner rosettes: retinoblastoma. True ependymal rosettes: ependymoma. Perivascular pseudorosettes: ependymoma. Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes): retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma, medulloblastoma.Lumen content: Flexner-Wintersteiner = clear. Ependymoma true rosette = clear. Perivascular pseudorosette = a blood vessel. Homer-Wright = a tangle of primitive neurites.Rosettes mark the cell line: neuronal differentiation (Homer-Wright) or ependymal (true / perivascular).Vessel in the center = ependymoma pseudorosette. Neurites in the center = Homer-Wright (medulloblastoma).⭐ Homer-Wright = neurite core (medulloblastoma, neuroblastoma); perivascular pseudorosette = vessel core (ependymoma); true rosette = clear lumen (ependymoma).

Deletion/mutation of NF2 on chr 22 if associated with NF2 syndrome.Gross: well circumscribed, solid or cystic with papillae. MeningiomaThe most common CNS tumor in adults; F>M (3:2). Deletion/mutation of NF2 on chr 22q, with or without NF2 syndrome. Location: attached to the meninges, often along the sagittal sinus. Often expresses progesterone, androgen or estrogen receptors, so it grows faster in pregnancy.Gross: nodule(s) compressing adjacent tissue without invasion. Micro: spindle-shaped cells; whorls and syncytia of epithelial-like cells; psammoma bodies.Usually good prognosis; some may be aggressive. Common cause of epilepsy.Dural-based, compresses rather than invades; whorls + psammoma bodies; female; hormone receptors.⭐ Meningioma: most common adult CNS tumor, F>M, NF2 (22q), parasagittal dural mass, whorls + psammoma bodies, PR/ER → grows in pregnancy.

Metastatic brain tumorsChildren and adults. Origin (descending order): lung carcinoma (all types), breast (HER-2+ and triple-negative), skin melanoma, renal clear cell, GI (colon, stomach), ovarian, testicular, bladder, thyroid, sarcoma.Brain: single or multiple well-demarcated nodules with perifocal edema ± secondary changes. PNS (nerve sheath) tumors: origin and classificationOrigin: Schwann cells. Location: peripheral nerves (often cutaneous) and nerve origins at the brain and spinal cord, where Schwann cells replace oligodendrocytes.Classification: neurofibroma (solitary, plexiform, diffuse); schwannoma; malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST).Neurofibromas belong with NF1; schwannomas with NF2.All derive from Schwann cells; MPNST is the malignant one.⭐ Nerve sheath tumors arise from Schwann cells: neurofibroma (solitary/plexiform/diffuse), schwannoma, MPNST.

Solitary (cutaneous) neurofibromaNeoplastic Schwann cells. Location: small cutaneous nerves; nerve roots, trunks and peripheral nerves. In NF1, appears in adolescence and becomes numerous.Gross: not encapsulated, infiltrates the nerve and cannot be separated from it, soft. Micro: proliferation of all nerve components (neoplastic Schwann cells + perineural-like cells, fibroblasts, collagen); serpentine pattern of cells, nuclei and collagen; embedded nerve trunks.Soft skin nodule.Unencapsulated; the nerve runs through it.⭐ Neurofibroma: unencapsulated, inseparable from the nerve, mixed cells in a serpentine pattern with incorporated axons.

Schwannoma (incl. vestibular schwannoma)Composed of Schwann cells. Subtype: vestibular schwannoma (misnomers: acoustic schwannoma, acoustic neuroma) of the vestibular branch of CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle. Bilateral = NF2.Gross: truly encapsulated, well circumscribed, attached to the nerve but can be separated, firm. Micro: Antoni A (dense spindle Schwann cells in fascicles with Verocay bodies: two parallel nuclear palisades separated by an anuclear zone) + Antoni B (loose hypocellular areas with myxoid matrix).Compresses adjacent structures (the nerve, brain or spinal cord). Vestibular: tinnitus, hearing loss. MRI: CPA mass.Encapsulated, pushes the nerve aside; Antoni A/B + Verocay bodies.⭐ Schwannoma: encapsulated, separable from the nerve, Antoni A (Verocay bodies) + Antoni B; vestibular CN VIII at the CPA causes tinnitus and hearing loss.

COMPARE: schwannoma vs neurofibromaSchwannoma: pure Schwann cells; NF2. Neurofibroma: Schwann cells + perineural-like cells + fibroblasts + collagen; NF1.Schwannoma: encapsulated round mass sitting eccentrically, with nerve fibers pushed to the side; separable; firm; Antoni A/B + Verocay. Neurofibroma: unencapsulated fusiform swelling with proliferating cells among nerve fibers; nerve fibers run through it; inseparable; soft; serpentine pattern.Schwannoma can be shelled out with the nerve preserved; neurofibroma cannot be separated from the nerve. Plexiform neurofibroma can become MPNST.Capsule + nerve pushed aside = schwannoma. No capsule + nerve inside = neurofibroma.⭐ Schwannoma pushes the nerve aside (encapsulated, separable, Verocay bodies); a neurofibroma has the nerve running through it (unencapsulated, inseparable, serpentine).

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)Autosomal dominant, with a high proportion of sporadic cases. Birth incidence 30–40/100,000. Tumor-suppressor NF1 gene on chr 17. Its product, neurofibromin, is a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) of the RAS/MAPK pathway; mutation lowers neurofibromin and activates RAS/MAPK.Criteria in order of appearance: (1) ≥6 café-au-lait spots (infancy); (2) axillary or inguinal freckling; (3) plexiform neurofibromas (progress to MPNST); (4) optic nerve gliomas; (5) pigmented iris nodules (Lisch nodules); (6) solitary cutaneous neurofibromas (adolescence, become numerous); (7) optic pathway gliomas (OPGs); (8) ↑ soft tissue sarcomas.Skin: café-au-lait spots, freckling, many cutaneous neurofibromas. Eye: Lisch nodules, optic glioma.Neurofibromas + café-au-lait + Lisch nodules = NF1 (chr 17, neurofibromin/RAS).⭐ NF1: AD, chr 17, neurofibromin (RAS-GAP); ≥6 café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, plexiform neurofibroma progressing to MPNST.

Its product, merlin (schwannomin), links the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane.Components: bilateral vestibular schwannomas; schwannomas of other cranial nerves; intracranial meningiomas; spinal tumors (ependymomas, meningiomas, schwannomas).Bilateral CPA masses: hearing loss, tinnitus.Bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2 (chr 22, merlin). NF2 tumors are schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas.⭐ NF2: AD, chr 22, merlin; bilateral vestibular schwannomas + meningiomas + spinal ependymomas.

TraumaPathology of head trauma, cerebral edema, raised ICP & brain herniation (Pathology component — Traumatic Brain and Spinal Cord Injuries) [Trauma · Pathology]· 24Each row = one lesion / process (or COMPARE row): etiology & pathogenesis · gross & micro buzzwords · clinical & imaging · the one differentiator

Edema type over time, by condition

  1. Ischemic stroke / global ischemiaCytotoxic first (Na+-K+ ATPase failure) → vasogenic (ischemic BBB damage)
  2. Subarachnoid hemorrhageCytotoxic (aneurysm rupture → severe ischemia) → vasogenic (endothelial damage)
  3. Traumatic brain injuryVasogenic (shearing → immediate diffuse BBB disruption) → ↑ ICP → neuronal ischemia → cytotoxic
  4. Intracranial hemorrhageVasogenic (clot inflammation) → ↑ ICP → microvascular compression → ischemia → cytotoxic
  5. OtherHyponatremia = osmotic · hydrocephalus = interstitial · tumor = vasogenic · infection = all three
Pathology component_Traumatic Brain and Spinal cord injuries (1)p.7Pathology component_Traumatic Brain and Spinal cord injuries (1)p.8

Uncal herniation — what gets compressed

  1. 1 · UncusMedial temporal lobe pushed against the free edge of the tentorium (pressure groove)
  2. 2 · CN IIIParasympathetic pupillary fibers → ipsilateral fixed, dilated (blown) pupil
  3. 3 · Ipsilateral peduncleContralateral weakness
  4. 4 · Contralateral peduncleLarge herniation pushes it against the tentorium (Kernohan notch) → ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan-Woltman)
  5. 5 · PCAIpsilateral PCA compressed → contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing
  6. 6 · BrainstemContinued descent → midbrain (coma) → pons → medulla; Duret hemorrhages

Transtentorial herniation — rostrocaudal stages

  1. Early diencephalicConfusion, poor concentration, sighs/yawns; stops obeying but still localizes to pain; small pupils, minimal reaction to light
  2. Late diencephalicProminent grasp reflex, deepening coma, loss of motor localization to pain, decorticate posturing (rubrospinal disinhibition)
  3. MidbrainIrregular pupils then fixed at mid-position; oculocephalic movements lost; decorticate → decerebrate rigidity
  4. PonsIrregular breathing; eye movements lost on caloric testing; reduced tone; tendon reflexes hard to elicit
  5. MedullaBreathing slows, gasping; adrenaline surge, pupils dilate temporarily; Cushing reflex (high BP, reflex bradycardia); autonomic function lost → BP drops → cardiac output ceases

Diffuse axonal injury — mechanism

  1. ForceAcceleration / deceleration → mechanical stretch of axons
  2. TearDirect tearing of axonal fibers → damaged fibers retract → axonal swellings (spheroids, retraction balls)
  3. TransportMicrotubules (stiffest part) break → axonal transport interrupted → β-APP accumulates → swelling
  4. Calcium↑ intracellular Ca2+ → apoptosis → axonal disconnection
  5. WhereMidline white matter: corpus callosum, subcortical white matter, gray–white junction

Subdural hematoma — CT evolution

  1. AcuteCrescent-shaped, hyperdense, concave toward the hemisphere; crosses sutures, not the midline; mass effect / midline shift
  2. Subacute (after 1 week)Isodense; sulci compressed/absent or displaced away from the inner table
  3. Chronic (>3–4 weeks)Hypodense compared with the brain; ventricular compression, displaced interhemispheric fissure

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) — definition & classificationAlteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force; any of: loss/decreased consciousness, loss of memory before (retrograde) or after (posttraumatic) the injury, neurologic deficit, altered mental state at time of injuryClinicopathologic classes: skull fracture (linear, basilar, comminuted, depressed, compound) · vascular injury (epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma; SAH & intracranial hemorrhage → CVD lecture) · parenchymal injury (concussion, contusion, laceration, diffuse axonal injury)Severity classified by the Glasgow coma scale — scores range 3–15Vascular injury = extra-axial bleeds (EDH / SDH); parenchymal = concussion, contusion, laceration, DAI⭐ TBI severity is graded with the Glasgow coma scale (3–15)

Vasogenic edemaBBB breakdown → ↑ vascular permeability → extracellular fluid. Early edema of TBI (mechanical shearing → immediate diffuse BBB disruption) and intracranial hemorrhage (inflammation from the clot & its breakdown products); infection (encephalitis, meningitis, abscess); peritumoral — tumor cells secrete substances that ↑ BBB permeability, ↓ tight junctions; follows cytotoxic edema in stroke & SAH (ischemic BBB / endothelial damage)Edematous brain: widened gyri with a flattened surface, narrowed sulciUnenhanced CT: vasogenic edema around a glioma; ↑ ICP → herniation to the contralateral side; effaced sulci, compressed ventricleExtracellular, BBB damage — the edema of tumors⭐ Peritumoral edema is vasogenic: tumor cells increase BBB permeability and decrease tight junctions

Cytotoxic edemaFailure of Na+-K+ ATPase → Na+ and Ca2+ influx through ligand-gated channels with water following → intracellular swelling. FIRST edema in acute ischemic stroke, global cerebral ischemia and SAH (aneurysm rupture → severe ischemic injury); LATER in TBI & ICH (vasogenic edema → ↑ ICP → neuronal ischemia / microvascular compression → cytotoxic); infection (microglial activation, leukocyte infiltration)Same gross picture: widened flattened gyri, narrowed sulciCT: loss of the normal gray–white matter differentiation, effaced sulci, compressed ventricle; large ischemic infarct with herniation; diffuse edema in global cerebral ischemia (diffuse hypoxic encephalopathy)Intracellular — loses the gray–white junction on CT⭐ Cytotoxic edema = Na+/K+-ATPase failure; on CT it erases the gray–white matter differentiation

Interstitial & osmotic edemaInterstitial: hydrocephalus — obstruction of CSF efflux → transependymal extravasation of CSF; meningitis may damage the CSF outflow pathway (infection can give vasogenic, cytotoxic AND interstitial). Osmotic: hyponatremia — water moves down an osmotic gradient into the CNSCSF crosses the ependyma into the surrounding parenchyma (interstitial)Context clues: hydrocephalus / meningitis (interstitial); low serum Na+ (osmotic)Interstitial = hydrocephalus; osmotic = hyponatremia⭐ Hydrocephalus causes interstitial edema by transependymal CSF extravasation

COMPARE — vasogenic vs cytotoxic edemaVasogenic: BBB damage / ↑ permeability → extracellular fluid (tumor, infection, early TBI & ICH). Cytotoxic: Na+-K+ ATPase failure → intracellular Na+, Ca2+ & water (ischemia, SAH)Both: widened gyri with flattened surface, narrowed sulci, compressed ventriclesOrder: ischemic stroke, global ischemia, SAH = cytotoxic → vasogenic; TBI, ICH = vasogenic → cytotoxic. After stroke: cytotoxic within hours, vasogenic 24–48 h later. CT: vasogenic around glioma; cytotoxic in large infarct with lost gray–white differentiationTumor → vasogenic; ischemia → cytotoxic first⭐ Ischemic stroke: cytotoxic edema within hours, vasogenic edema 24–48 h later

Brain herniation — overviewDisplacement of brain tissue past rigid dural folds (falx, tentorium) or through openings in the skull because of increased intracranial pressureMajor types: uncal, transtentorial/central, subfalcine, tonsillar (+ ascending transtentorial and transdural/transcranial in the clinical session)Progressive ↓ consciousness: confusion, restlessness, lethargy, drowsiness, stupor → coma → brain death; medullary involvement → central respiratory failure and deathSupratentorial mass → uncal, central, subfalcine, transdural; infratentorial mass → ascending transtentorial, tonsillar⭐ Herniation = brain pushed past the falx/tentorium or through skull openings by raised ICP

COMPARE — decorticate vs decerebrate posturingDecorticate: bilateral damage rostral to the midbrain, lesion above the red nucleus (rubrospinal tract disinhibited). Decerebrate: damage to motor tracts caudal to the midbrain, lesion at or below the red nucleusDecorticate: flexion of elbows & wrists, arms supine ('arms point to the cortex'). Decerebrate: extension of elbows & wrists with pronation ('E = extension')In transtentorial herniation: decorticate in the late diencephalic stage → decerebrate in the midbrain stage as the rubrospinal tract fails; GCS motor 3 (flexion) vs 2 (extension)The red nucleus is the dividing line⭐ Decorticate = above the red nucleus; decerebrate = at/below it

Epidural hematoma (EDH)Temporal skull fracture → rupture of the middle meningeal artery → blood separates dura from periosteum → slowly expanding hematoma compresses the brainBetween dura and skull; torn middle meningeal vessels lift the dura off the skull → epidural clotInitial LOC → transient complete recovery (lucid interval, 14–21%, not pathognomonic) → rapid deterioration; ipsilateral pupil dilation (uncal herniation, CN III); Cushing triad — ↑ systolic BP, slow HR, irregular breathing. CT: hyperdense extra-axial biconvex / lens-shaped mass, temporoparietal; does not cross suture lines (dura fused to calvarium at sutures)Arterial, lens-shaped, stops at sutures⭐ EDH: middle meningeal artery, lucid interval, biconvex and does not cross sutures

Subdural hematoma (SDH)Tear of bridging veins → blood between dura and arachnoid over the cerebral convexities. Acute: direct cranial trauma, coagulopathy, falls; chronic: trivial injury, coagulopathy. Risk: older adults (cerebral atrophy stretches bridging veins), infants (thin-walled bridging veins)Between dura and arachnoid; dura reflected back reveals the clotSmall — asymptomatic. Large acute (minutes–hours): stupor/coma, hemiparesis, unilateral pupil enlargement. Chronic (days–weeks): headache, progressive mental status change ± focal signs; infants: head enlargement, vomiting, convulsions. CT: acute crescent-shaped hyperdense, concave toward the hemisphere, crosses sutures but not the midline; subacute (>1 wk) isodense; chronic (>3–4 wk) hypodenseVenous, crescent, crosses sutures; elderly & infants⭐ SDH: torn bridging veins, crescent that crosses sutures but not the midline

COMPARE — epidural vs subdural hematomaEDH: temporal fracture → middle meningeal artery (arterial). SDH: bridging veins (venous); elderly atrophy, infants, coagulopathy (warfarin, alcohol)EDH: dura ↔ skull. SDH: dura ↔ arachnoid, over the convexitiesEDH: lucid interval then rapid deterioration (hours). SDH: longer interval (low-pressure venous bleed grows slowly; days–weeks if chronic). CT: EDH biconvex/lenticular, does not cross sutures; SDH crescent, concave toward brain, crosses sutures not midline. EDH often without underlying brain damage (better prognosis); SDH often with underlying cerebral damageLens + respects sutures = EDH; crescent + crosses sutures = SDH⭐ EDH is lens-shaped and respects sutures; SDH is crescent-shaped and crosses them

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI)Severe TBI from shearing forces: direct impact, fast acceleration/deceleration (motor vehicle accident, passenger ejected), falls, blunt assault. Stretch tears axons → retraction → spheroids; microtubules break → interrupted axonal transport → β-APP accumulates; ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → apoptosis → disconnectionMidline white matter: corpus callosum, subcortical white matter, gray–white junction; gross petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum. Micro: axonal swelling — beading, retraction balls, spheroids (silver stain), axonal disconnectionConsider if GCS <8 for >6 hours without a mass lesion; severe DAI: unconscious immediately, stays comatose or persistent vegetative state. CT normal in 50–89%; MRI = study of choice (petechial hemorrhages in corpus callosum, temporal/parietal corticomedullary junction)Coma with a normal CT and no mass lesion⭐ DAI: GCS <8 for >6 h without a mass lesion; retraction balls / β-APP; MRI is the study of choice

Rostral-caudal deterioration — sign by level

  1. Bihemispheric / early diencephalicCheyne-Stokes; small (~2 mm) reactive pupils; reflex eye movements intact; localizes to pain
  2. Late diencephalicAs above, but pain → decorticate (flexor) posturing
  3. MidbrainFixed midsize (~5 mm) pupils; reflex adduction impaired; decerebrate (extensor) posturing
  4. Pons (pontomesencephalic)Kussmaul (rapid deep) breathing; fixed midsize pupils; loss of abduction and adduction
  5. MedullaShallow slow breathing → agonal gasps; no motor response or only leg flexion; apnea

Raised ICP — stepwise management

  1. 1 · PositionHead of bed 15–30°, head midline
  2. 2 · Airway / ventilationHyperventilation lowers PaCO2 → vasoconstriction (fast, fades 6–24 h; avoid PaCO2 <20 mmHg)
  3. 3 · PhysiologyControl sedation, analgesia, fever, seizures, blood pressure
  4. 4 · HyperosmolarMannitol — check contraindications (dehydration, acute intracranial bleed, pulmonary edema, CHF, anuria)
  5. 5 · SurgeryEvacuate clot/mass, ICP monitoring, intraventricular drain
  6. 6 · RefractoryBarbiturate coma; hypothermia (no proven benefit); NOT steroids in TBI

1 / 2

Brain death — diagnostic sequence

  1. PrerequisitesAcute CNS catastrophe; no confounding medical condition; no drugs/sedatives; core temp >36 °C; SBP >100 mmHg
  2. ExamComa, no brain-originating motor response, absent pupillary/corneal/oculocephalic/oculovestibular/jaw/gag/cough reflexes
  3. Apnea testNo respiratory effort
  4. ObservationAt least 6 h (longer in children and after cardiac arrest)
  5. Ancillary (if exam not possible)Angiography, EEG, transcranial Doppler, scintigraphy — empty skull

TBI — definition, causes & classificationAlteration in brain function or other evidence of brain pathology caused by an external force; intoxication or medical illness do NOT exclude TBI. Causes: head struck by object, head strikes object, acceleration/deceleration without impact, penetrating foreign body, blast; falls = most common, then road traffic injuriesClosed (more common) vs penetrating (violation of skull AND dura). Extra-axial (inside skull, outside brain): EDH, SDH, SAH, intraventricular hemorrhage. Intra-axial (in the brain): intracerebral hemorrhage, contusion, DAIShared intracranial-hemorrhage symptoms: headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, somnolence, seizure; spectrum from alert to moribundPenetrating = dura breached⭐ Falls are the single most common cause of TBI, followed by road traffic injuries

ConcussionTransient disturbance of brain function from head injury, usually a blow; likely mild diffuse axonal injury and excitotoxic neuronal injuryNo structural brain abnormality directly or on imaging; if a contusion is present it is called a contusion; hemorrhage on CT → no longer mild TBITrauma-induced alteration in mental status ± LOC: headache, dizziness, confusion, slurred speech, vomiting, disorientation, irritability, amnesia, clumsiness, visual disturbance; severe: prolonged coma, seizures, posturing. Single concussion → most athletes recover fullyNormal imaging⭐ Concussion has no structural abnormality on imaging

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)Multiple (even minor) concussions → about 3% develop CTE; first described in boxers (dementia pugilistica, 'punch-drunk')Structural neurodegenerative changes similar to Alzheimer disease — cortical atrophy; listed as an NDDMemory problems, impaired judgment & decision making, personality change, parkinsonismRepetitive concussion → neurodegeneration⭐ Repeated concussions → CTE (dementia pugilistica) with AD-like atrophy and parkinsonism

Laceration = tearing of cerebral tissue and pia-arachnoid overlying a contusionLOC longer than with concussion; focal neurologic deficits, confusion, impaired consciousness; herniation in severe cases; may → severe residual deficit or deathVisible bruise (vs concussion: none); laceration = pia torn⭐ Contusion = coup/contrecoup cortical bruise at gyral crests; laceration also tears the pia-arachnoid

Diffuse axonal (traumatic axonal) injury — clinicalWidespread axonal disruption from shear and stretch during acceleration/deceleration (severe rotational shearing forces)Imaging may be normal or show tiny scattered white-matter hemorrhages (corpus callosum, basal ganglia); histology — torn axonsUnconscious from the moment of injury, no lucid interval; persistent coma / vegetative state / severe disability until deathMost common cause of coma without an intracranial hematoma⭐ DAI is the most common cause of coma without a hematoma and of severe disability after head injury

Epidural hematoma — clinical & managementTorn dural vessels — middle meningeal artery (also meningeal vein or dural sinus); often temporal bone fractureCT: lenticular / biconvex hyperdensity; may lack underlying brain damage → better prognosis than other TBILucid interval, then rapid deterioration (arterial); headache, confusion, somnolence, seizures, focal deficit hours after injury; ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing); respiratory depression → death unless evacuated. Rx: large/symptomatic → emergent surgical evacuation; small → watchful waitingLucid interval + lens shape⭐ EDH: lucid interval then rapid arterial deterioration — emergent evacuation

Subdural hematoma — clinicalBridging veins (cortex → superior sagittal sinus) or cerebral laceration; MVA, falls; elderly after minimal/no trauma (atrophy stretches veins); shaken baby; clotting abnormalities (warfarin, alcohol)CT: crescent-shaped hyperdensity concave toward the brain (rarely lens-shaped); often with underlying cerebral damageLike EDH (headache, confusion, somnolence, seizures, focal deficit) but longer interval — low-pressure venous bleed grows slowly → delayed days–weeks. Case 1: 85-y man fell off bed yesterday, headache & vomiting today. Rx: large/symptomatic → urgent surgery, otherwise close monitoringElderly + delayed symptoms + crescent⭐ SDH is venous and slow — symptoms delayed days to weeks, classically in the elderly

Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (tSAH)Head injury from a fall or road traffic accident; bleeding into the subarachnoid space; less blood than aneurysmal ruptureCT: blood in sulci over the cerebral convexities; usually no surgery neededThunderclap headache, ↓ consciousness, hemiparesis, vomiting, neck stiffness, seizure; ↑ ICP mainly by blocking CSF outflow from the 3rd & 4th ventricles. Headache before the fall → CT/angiogram to exclude aneurysmConvexity sulci (traumatic) vs basal cisterns (aneurysm)⭐ Traumatic SAH sits in convexity sulci; aneurysmal SAH fills the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures

Basilar skull fractureFracture of a skull-base bone (cribriform plate, orbital plate of frontal, petrous & squamous temporal, sphenoid, occipital); most often through the temporal bone → high risk of EDH (weak bone, near middle meningeal artery & vein)Battle sign (retroauricular/mastoid ecchymosis, 1–3 days); raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis, 1–3 days); hemotympanum (blue-purple TM on otoscopy, within hours — petrous ridge); clear CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea; halo / double-ring sign (not specific)Case 2: MVA with these signs on head exam and otoscopyBattle sign + raccoon eyes + hemotympanum⭐ Basilar skull fracture: Battle sign, raccoon eyes (1–3 days), hemotympanum (hours), CSF leak

Raised ICP after acute TBI — clinicalExpanding hematoma, tumor, edemaExam: papilledema; systemic: hypertension, sinus bradycardia, respiratory depression; uncommon: pulmonary edema, Cushing ulcers (GI ulceration & hemorrhage)Altered mental status, nausea & vomiting, blurred vision, focal deficit, seizures, coma, death. CT/MRI shows hematoma/tumor; lumbar puncture is contraindicatedNever LP with raised ICP⭐ Raised ICP: papilledema + hypertension, bradycardia, respiratory depression; LP contraindicated

Raised ICP — managementInitial: head of bed 15–30°, head midline (venous drainage); airway + hyperventilation (↓ PaCO2 → vasoconstriction → ↓ CBF; works fast but fades over 6–24 h; PaCO2 <20 mmHg → ischemia); control sedation, analgesia, fever, seizures; BP neither too high nor too lowMannitol (hyperosmolar, most used) — CI: severe dehydration, acute intracranial bleeding, pulmonary edema, CHF, anuria with severe renal disease. Surgery: evacuate clot/mass, ICP monitoring, intraventricular drainRefractory: barbiturate coma (↓ brain metabolism & CBF; many AEs; no reliable neuro exam for days); hypothermia (no proven outcome benefit). Dexamethasone treats tumor edema — no benefit in TBI or spontaneous ICH. Case 3: GCS 6, SAH, basal cracklesSteroids for tumor edema only⭐ Corticosteroids help tumor edema but are of no benefit in TBI; check mannitol contraindications (pulmonary edema, acute bleed)

Other herniations — central, ascending transtentorial, transduralCentral: entire hemisphere herniates across the tentorium. Ascending transtentorial: cerebellum & brainstem herniate upward through the tentorium (infratentorial mass). Transdural/transcranial: brain herniates outward (damaged skull, post-craniotomy with ↑ ICP)Pathways: supratentorial mass → uncal, central, subfalcine, transdural; infratentorial mass → ascending transtentorial, tonsillarProgressive ↓ consciousness → coma → brain deathUpward = infratentorial mass; outward = skull defect⭐ Ascending transtentorial herniation comes from an infratentorial (posterior fossa) mass

Rostral-caudal deterioration (downward transtentorial herniation)Expanding supratentorial mass first gives local deficits, then presses on the diencephalon → predictable sequence (steps may be skipped in rapid lesions)Track 5 variables: consciousness, pupils, respiration, vestibulo-ocular function, motor response. Reflex levels: pupillary light = midbrain & CN III; eye movements & corneal = pons; respiratory & pharyngeal = medullaEarly diencephalic: small (~2 mm) reactive pupils, intact reflex eye movements, localizes. Late diencephalic: decorticate. Midbrain: fixed midsize (~5 mm) pupils, impaired adduction, decerebrate. Pons/medulla: fixed midsize, loss of abduction AND adduction, no motor response or only leg flexionMidsize fixed pupils (herniation) vs pinpoint (isolated pontine lesion)⭐ Herniation to the pons gives midsize fixed pupils because CN III parasympathetics are lost too — an isolated pontine lesion gives pinpoint pupils

Respiratory patterns in comaBihemispheral: Cheyne-Stokes (cyclic, ending in a brief apnea) — bihemispheral damage or metabolic suppression; light comaPontomesencephalic: rapid deep Kussmaul breathing — metabolic acidosis, pontomesencephalic lesionsMedulla: shallow, slow, regular (metabolic / drug depression of medullary centers); agonal gasps = lower brainstem damage, terminal pattern. Cases 5 & 6: localize from breathing + pupils + motorAgonal gasps = medulla⭐ Cheyne-Stokes = bihemispheric; Kussmaul = pontomesencephalic; agonal gasps = medulla

Clinical brain deathComplete & irreversible loss of cerebral and brainstem function. Prerequisites: acute CNS catastrophe; exclude confounders (electrolyte, acid–base, endocrine, shock); no drug intoxication / in-hospital sedatives; core temperature >36 °C; systolic BP >100 mmHg (vasopressors allowed)Exam: coma; no brain-originating motor response (incl. posturing, seizures); pupils midposition (3.5–4 mm), no light reflex; absent corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, jaw jerk, gag, cough, sucking/rooting (neonates); apnea testObservation ≥6 hours (longer in children, after cardiac arrest). Path lecture: cardiac activity preserved, respiration maintained artificially; widespread cortical destruction + global brainstem damage; pupils bilaterally dilated and unreactiveAll prerequisites met before the exam⭐ Brain death: exclude confounders (temp >36 °C, SBP >100, no sedatives), then coma + absent brainstem reflexes + apnea, observe ≥6 h

Spinal cord injury — complete vs incompleteTrauma or non-trauma; disrupts brain–cord–end-organ communication → sensory, motor, autonomic dysfunction; traumatic SCI mainly young adults <40 yTracts: spinothalamic tract = pain & temperature; dorsal columns = vibration, proprioception, pressure, light touch; corticospinal tract = motorComplete (incl. transection): no sensation or movement below the injury. Incomplete: some preserved. Above C6 → quadriplegic, dependent; below T1 → paraplegic, more independentAny sparing below the level = incomplete⭐ SCI above C6 → quadriplegia; below T1 → paraplegia

Vascular & strokePathology of Cerebrovascular Diseases [Vascular · Pathology]· 28Each row = one lesion / process (or COMPARE row): etiology & pathogenesis · gross & micro buzzwords · clinical & imaging · the one differentiator

Cascade of cerebral ischemia

  1. Ischemia↓ flow (focal or global) → core of infarction + surrounding penumbra
  2. Pump failureNa+-K+ ATPase fails → Na+ and Ca2+ influx through ligand-gated channels, water follows → cytotoxic edema (within hours)
  3. BBB damageIschemic injury to the blood-brain barrier → vasogenic edema (24–48 h)
  4. PenumbraReversibly dysfunctional rim progresses to infarction unless flow is restored — target of revascularization

Global ischemia — microscopic timeline

  1. Early (6–12 h)Red neurons; later changes in astrocytes and oligodendroglia
  2. Subacute (24 h–2 wk)Tissue necrosis, influx of macrophages, vessel proliferation, reactive gliosis
  3. Repair (>2 wk)Loss of normal CNS architecture, gliosis
Pathology of Cerebrovascular Diseases
p.15

Cerebral infarct — gross & micro evolution

  1. <6 hNo changes evident
  2. 6–12 hEosinophilic neuronal necrosis (red neurons)
  3. Up to 48 hPale, soft, swollen; gray–white junction indistinct; neutrophil emigration rises then falls
  4. 48–72 hPhagocytes (activated microglia) visible as foamy macrophages
  5. 2–10 daysGelatinous and friable; by 1 week reactive astrocytes and new vessels at the periphery
  6. 10 days–3 weeksTissue liquefies → fluid-filled cavity; phagocytes predominate by 2–3 weeks
  7. MonthsDense meshwork of glial fibers + new capillaries + perivascular connective tissue (remote infarct)

1 / 4

Ischemic stroke — CT evolution

  1. First hoursNoncontrast CT first (availability); DWI MRI already detects ischemia within 20–30 min
  2. 12–24 hIndistinct low attenuation in a vascular distribution
  3. >24 hBetter circumscribed; mass effect peaks at 3–5 days
  4. ~72 hContrast enhancement as mass effect wanes
  5. 2–4 weeksMass effect gone
  6. >4 weeksWell-circumscribed low-attenuation lesion, no enhancement
Pathology of Cerebrovascular Diseasesp.20Pathology of Cerebrovascular Diseasesp.21
1 / 2

Intracerebral hemorrhage — CT density over time

  1. ImmediatelyHyperdense (protein of whole blood, mostly hemoglobin)
  2. Up to ~3 daysBecomes denser as the clot dehydrates
  3. After day 3Density falls from the outside in — clot appears to shrink, invisible over several weeks
  4. ~2 monthsOnly a small hypodensity may remain
Pathology of Cerebrovascular Diseases
p.37

Hypertension → intraparenchymal hemorrhage

  1. Chronic hypertensionAccelerated atherosclerosis (large arteries); hyaline arteriolosclerosis (small arteries)
  2. Vessel wallAtrophy of the outer muscular layer of small penetrating vessels → loss of wall integrity
  3. Charcot-BouchardMicroaneurysms form
  4. RuptureGanglionic bleed — putamen (50–60%), thalamus, pons, cerebellum

COMPARE — stroke vs transient ischemic attack (TIA)Stroke (CVA): neurologic signs explained by a vascular mechanism, acute onset, persisting >24 h OR infarction demonstrated. TIA: all signs resolve within 24 h without infarction on imagingTwo mechanisms of stroke: ischemia/hypoxia (global or focal) and hemorrhageImaging decides: any infarct on imaging = strokeInfarct on imaging = stroke regardless of duration⭐ TIA resolves within 24 h with NO infarct on imaging

Global cerebral ischemia (diffuse hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy)Generalized ↓ cerebral perfusion or ↓ O2-carrying capacity: cardiac arrest, MI, asphyxiation, respiratory failure, shock, severe hypotension, CO / cyanide poisoning. Most sensitive cells: hippocampal pyramidal neurons, cerebellar Purkinje cells, cortical pyramidal neurons (layers III & V)Edema; multifocal or diffuse laminar necrosis. Micro: red neurons (6–12 h) → necrosis, macrophages, vessel proliferation, reactive gliosis (24 h–2 wk) → loss of architecture, gliosis (>2 wk)Often fatal; persistent vegetative state; brain death. CT: diffuse edema, loss of gray–white differentiationSelective vulnerability + laminar necrosis⭐ Most vulnerable to hypoxia: hippocampal pyramidal neurons, Purkinje cells, cortical layers III & V

Ischemic stroke — etiologyEmbolism: cardiac mural thrombi (atrial fibrillation, MI, valvular disease); artery-to-artery from carotid atheroma; paradoxical thromboemboli (PFO / ASD). In situ thrombosis: aortic arch, common & internal carotid, vertebral, basilarOther: vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa; syphilis, TB); hypercoagulable (prothrombin gene mutation, Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid Ab, malignancy, DIC); sickle cell; hyperviscosity (polycythemia vera, Waldenström); vasospasm (SAH, meningitis); drugs (cocaine, amphetamines, marijuana, SSRIs, pseudoephedrine)Usually sudden focal deficit in a vascular territoryEmbolus vs in-situ thrombus⭐ Embolic sources: cardiac mural thrombi (AF, MI, valves), carotid atheroma, paradoxical emboli via PFO/ASD

Ischemic stroke — imagingMost acute strokes first imaged with noncontrast CT (availability); diffusion-weighted MRI more sensitive and specific — detects ischemia within 20–30 minCT 12–24 h: indistinct low attenuation in a vascular distribution. >24 h: better circumscribed, mass effect peaks 3–5 days, gone by 2–4 wk. ~72 h: contrast enhancement as mass effect wanes. >4 wk: well-circumscribed low-attenuation lesion, no enhancementCT may be normal at 2 h while DWI is already positiveDWI first positive; CT lags⭐ Mass effect of an infarct peaks at 3–5 days; DWI MRI shows ischemia within 20–30 min

Ischemic stroke — morphology (cerebral infarct)Sustained ischemia → liquefactive necrosis; spontaneous or therapeutic dissolution of the occlusive material → reperfusion → secondary hemorrhagic transformationGross: <6 h no change; 48 h pale, soft, swollen, indistinct gray–white junction; 2–10 d gelatinous & friable; 10 d–3 wk liquefies → fluid-filled cystic cavity. Micro: red neurons 6–12 h; neutrophils up to 48 h; foamy macrophages (activated microglia) 48–72 h; reactive astrocytes & new vessels at periphery by 1 wk; phagocytes predominate 2–3 wk; months: dense glial meshwork + new capillariesSubacute infarct vs remote (cavitated) infarctBrain infarcts liquefy and cavitate⭐ Red neurons appear at 6–12 h; foamy macrophages at 48–72 h; cystic cavity by 10 days–3 weeks

Hemorrhagic: reperfusion after spontaneous or therapeutic dissolution/fragmentation of the occlusive materialPale: liquefactive necrosis without blood. Lacunar strokeOcclusion of a small end artery; chronic hypertension → arteriolosclerosis of small penetrating arteries (small vessel disease). Mechanisms: lipohyalinosis (most common), microatheroma at the origin, small emboli. Risk: hypertension, age, diabetes, hyperlipidemiaLake-like cystic spaces 5–15 mm (<15 mm), single or multiple, in putamen, globus pallidus, thalamus, internal capsule, deep white matter, caudate, pons; tissue loss surrounded by gliosisPure motor (posterior limb of internal capsule / pons; lenticulostriate artery); pure sensory (ventral thalamus); ataxic hemiparesis (ventral pons / internal capsule); dysarthria–clumsy hand (ventral pons / genu). CT: small low-density cyst 5–15 mm<15 mm deep infarct in a hypertensive⭐ Lacunes: <15 mm deep infarcts from hypertensive lipohyalinosis; pure motor stroke in the internal capsule

Hemorrhagic stroke — causes by locationTrauma: frontal & anterior temporal parenchyma, SAH, subdural/epidural. Hypertension: putamen, globus pallidus, thalamus, cerebellum, pons. Aneurysm: subarachnoid, intraparenchymal, rarely subduralAVM: lobar, intraventricular, subarachnoid. Amyloid angiopathy: lobar. Cavernous angioma: intraparenchymal. Coagulopathy: any. Cocaine, amphetamine: any, lobar, subarachnoidGanglionic (deep) = hypertension; lobar = amyloid angiopathyLocation points to the cause⭐ Deep ganglionic bleed = hypertension; lobar bleed in the elderly = amyloid angiopathy

Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhageChronic hypertension → accelerated atherosclerosis (large arteries), hyaline arteriolosclerosis (small arteries); Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms — atrophy of the outer muscular layer of small penetrating vessels → microaneurysms ruptureGanglionic: putamen (50–60%), thalamus, pons, cerebellar hemispheres (rarely); arteriolosclerotic vessel wall; hemorrhagic necrosis in PCA-derived territories (thalamus/subthalamus)Abrupt focal deficit worsening over 30–90 min; reactive hypertension; ↓ consciousness; ↑ ICP (projectile vomiting, headache); seizures rare. Putamen: contralateral hemiplegia, slurred speech, eyes deviate away from lesion. Thalamus: hemiplegia, severe hemisensory loss, aphasia/neglect, ocular signs. Pons: decerebrate rigidity, pinpoint (1 mm) reactive pupils, mostly fatal. CT: hyperdense bloodPutamen most common; pinpoint pupils = pons⭐ Hypertensive bleeds: putamen most common; Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms rupture

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)Trauma = most frequent cause; ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm = most common spontaneous cause; also ICH rupturing into ventricles, vascular malformation, hematologic, tumors. Rupture spontaneous or with acute ↑ ICP (straining at stool, sexual orgasm)Blood pooling in cerebral sulci & basal cisterns; pink CSFThunderclap headache ('worst headache I've ever had'), rapid LOC, vomiting, stiff neck. Dx: noncontrast CT; CSF — similar RBCs over several tubes, xanthochromia. Complications: rebleeding, seizures, communicating hydrocephalus (arachnoid granulations), vasospasm, hyponatremia (SIADH / cerebral salt wasting); cytotoxic → vasogenic edemaXanthochromia; vasospasm⭐ SAH: thunderclap headache; xanthochromia proves blood was in CSF before the tap

Brainstem Rule of 4s4 midline structures (M): Motor pathway (corticospinal), Medial lemniscus, MLF, Motor nucleus (CN 3, 4, 6, 12). 4 side structures (S): Spinocerebellar, Spinothalamic, Sensory nucleus of V, Sympathetic. CN 3-4 midbrain, 5-8 pons, 9-12 medulla.Medial syndromes = contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral proprioception loss + ipsilateral motor CN (3/4, 6, 12). Lateral syndromes = ipsilateral Horner, ipsilateral face pain/temp, contralateral body pain/temp, ipsilateral ataxia + CN 5,7,8 (pons) or 9,10,11 (medulla).Level = which CN; medial vs lateral = M vs S tracts⭐ Rule of 4s: midline motor nuclei = CN 3, 4, 6, 12; CN 5, 7, 8 = lateral pons; CN 9, 10, 11 = lateral medulla

Vascular & strokeStroke types, workup & management (CVD Workshop · Stroke post-session) [Vascular · Clinical & pharmacology]· 28Each row = one stroke type / topic or a COMPARE row: features, investigations, management & drugs, differentiator; cards = acute algorithms

Acute ischemic stroke — algorithm (TIME is BRAIN)

  1. RecognizeSudden focal deficit; history (onset time, pattern F/A/L), vitals (BP, pulse rhythm), neuro exam
  2. 1. Noncontrast CTTop priority — rule out hemorrhage (thrombolytics are contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke); normal CT does not rule out ischemia
  3. 2. Immediate labsCBC + platelets, PT/PTT/INR, cardiac markers, electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose, lipids, O2 sat
  4. 3. ReperfusionNo bleed and within 3-4.5 h of last symptom-free → tPA protocol (restore flow to ischemic but not yet infarcted brain)
  5. 4. ThrombectomyMechanical thrombectomy (endovascular) — alternative, up to 24 h for large-vessel anterior circulation clots
  6. 5. Start therapyLow-dose aspirin + statin immediately once hemorrhage excluded (any degree of stenosis)
  7. 6. BPLower only if > 220/120; tPA candidates need < 185/110 (labetalol, nitroprusside, CCB)
  8. 7. Look for sourceCT/MR angiography, echocardiogram, carotid ultrasound, ECG (AF)

tPA — key contraindications

  1. BleedingActive bleeding anywhere, incl. hemorrhagic stroke
  2. ImagingMultilobar infarcts
  3. BP> 185/110 mm Hg if it cannot be adequately lowered (labetalol etc.) — e.g. 200/110 excludes
  4. Recent eventsHead trauma, prior stroke or MI within 3 months; GI bleed within 3 weeks; major surgery within 2 weeks
  5. CoagulationElevated INR or PTT (e.g., heparin or warfarin — heparin 24 h ago excludes); platelets < 100,000/mm3
  6. Not a contraindicationIschemic signs, negative CT, presentation within 3 h — these are the indications
Fusion Session - Workshop - Cerebrovascular Diseases - Session PDFp.19Stroke_Ischemic & Hemorrhagic_Post-Session with Answersp.46
1 / 2

Intracerebral hemorrhage — acute management

  1. 1. Noncontrast CTImmediate head CT
  2. 2. ↓ICPRaise head of bed, hyperventilation (acutely), osmotic diuresis, surgical evacuation of bleed
  3. 3. DrugsAnticonvulsants; antihypertensives (BP control prevents recurrent bleeds)
  4. 4. No antithromboticsNo role for anticoagulation or aspirin
  5. 5. DefinitiveTreat an aneurysm surgically if present and possible (clipping or coiling)
Stroke_Ischemic & Hemorrhagic_Post-Session with Answersp.49Fusion Session - Workshop - Cerebrovascular Diseases - Session PDFp.20
1 / 2

Subarachnoid hemorrhage — management

  1. 1. Noncontrast CTBest first step (positive ~6 h)
  2. 2. LP if CT normalHigh opening pressure, RBCs not decreasing tube 1→4, xanthochromia (pink/yellow, Hb breakdown; still present > 12 h)
  3. 3. ICU careBedrest, analgesia, pneumatic compression stockings, discontinue antithrombotics
  4. 4. BPOptimal target unclear: lowering ↓ rebleed but may ↑ infarction
  5. 5. Surgery earlyClipping (open) or endoscopic coiling of the aneurysm
  6. 6. VasospasmNimodipine (calcium channel blocker); watch hydrocephalus/↑ICP

1 / 3

Secondary prevention after ischemic stroke / TIA

  1. AntiplateletAspirin daily; clopidogrel if stroke on aspirin (P2Y12 blockers first-line for secondary stroke prevention); aspirin + dipyridamole superior to aspirin alone
  2. StatinMost patients benefit from a statin
  3. BP< 130/80 mm Hg
  4. LifestyleQuit smoking, exercise, weight loss; control diabetes; diet
  5. AF (embolic)Warfarin or non-vitamin K oral anticoagulant + rhythm conversion or rate control (β-blockers)
  6. Carotid stenosisAspirin + statin; endarterectomy only if symptomatic and stenosis > 70%

Cerebrovascular disease — frameworksFocal (one artery → e.g. right-arm weakness) vs global (↓flow to most of brain → LOC, coma, confusion). Ischemia (↓flow/O2) vs bleeding (compression; headache, vomiting, confusion from ↑ICP). Transient (TIA) vs permanent (stroke, neuronal death).Location in the circulation is key to therapy & prognosis.Rehab: physical & occupational therapy.Focal vs global; ischemia vs bleed; transient vs permanent⭐ Most cerebrovascular disease is focal; global hypoperfusion gives LOC/coma/confusion

Stroke — definition, types & epidemiologyNeurological deficit from injury/death of brain cells in a localized area when cerebral circulation is disrupted (abrupt vascular insufficiency or bleeding). Ischemic >80%: embolism, thrombosis (large vessel, lacunar), systemic hypoperfusion (watershed), TIA. Hemorrhagic <20%: ICH (spontaneous/hypertensive), SAH, AVM.Usually thrombus or embolus.—Men > women at younger ages, reversed > 75 yrs; Blacks & Hispanics higher risk; common cause of mortality & disability⭐ Ischemic strokes are >80% of strokes in the US; hemorrhagic <20%

Risk factors — modifiable vs non-modifiableModifiable: hypertension, obesity, smoking, cardiac disease, atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, hypercholesterolemia, atherosclerosis, diabetes, drug use (cocaine, IV drugs), hypercoagulable states (uncommon). Non-modifiable: family history of MI/stroke, age > 60, male sex, ethnicity (African American, Hispanic, Asian).Lipid profile, glucose, ECG (AF), carotid ultrasound.Thrombotic strokes linked to modifiable risk factors in >90%: weight loss, exercise, BP & lipid reduction, smoking cessation, treat AF.Uncommon causes: craniocervical dissection (young), venous sinus thrombosis, vasculitis, sickle cell disease⭐ Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor (No. 1 for atherosclerosis, ICH and aneurysm)

Large vessel thrombotic strokeClot of platelets + fibrin on atherosclerotic plaque occludes a large artery (MCA most often). Atherosclerosis risk factors in order: HTN, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, inflammation. Rarer: vasculitis, amyloid. Stuttering time course.Noncontrast CT (rule out bleed) → CT/MR angiography; carotid US, echo, ECG.Aspirin low-dose + statin immediately; tPA ≤ 4.5 h; mechanical thrombectomy ≤ 24 h for large-vessel anterior clots. Long term: aspirin (clopidogrel if stroke on aspirin), statin, BP < 130/80.Stuttering onset vs embolic maximal-at-onset⭐ Thrombotic strokes: atherosclerosis + clot, MCA most often, stuttering course; aspirin + statin once bleed excluded

Small vessel / lacunar strokeSmall penetrating arteries (off MCA, PCA) → lipohyalinosis (HTN, diabetes, old age): endothelial damage, wall thickening/ballooning → occlusion. Small infarcts 2-20 mm in deep white matter, basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus, pons; appear as little holes. Symptoms develop over hours to a few days.CT/MRI: tiny lacunes.Same ischemic-stroke pathway; control HTN & diabetes.Syndromes: contralateral pure motor (face=arm=leg), pure sensory, sensorimotor (15-20%), ataxic hemiparesis, clumsy hand-dysarthria (rare); NO cortical signs⭐ Lacunar infarcts: lipohyalinosis from hypertension → pure motor/sensory face=arm=leg with no cortical signs

Embolic strokeClot, fat, cholesterol plaque or air lodges in a large vessel (usually MCA; small vessels too small). Sources: heart (damaged valves, poorly mobile LV, dilated LA, atrial fibrillation) and carotid artery plaque (carotid stenosis, bruit). Sudden, maximal at onset; may have multiple embolic events.Echocardiogram (atrial clots), ECG (AF), carotid ultrasound.Prevent recurrence: AF → warfarin or DOACs + rhythm conversion or rate control (β-blockers); carotid stenosis → aspirin + statin; endarterectomy only if symptomatic and stenosis > 70%.Normal CT + murmur/AF/irregular pulse → embolic⭐ Most common embolic sources = heart (AF) and carotid artery; onset is sudden and maximal

Transient ischemic attack (TIA)Transient focal neurologic dysfunction from focal brain, spinal cord or retinal ischemia without acute infarction; usually embolic (minute particles that occlude then degrade); most last ≤ 5 min. TIA 1/1000 vs stroke 0.6/1000; 3-4% go on to stroke.Evaluate fully like stroke; MRI shows no residual damage; carotid ultrasound, echo, ECG; rule out hypoglycemia, MI, heart failure, anemia.Treat and follow closely; heparin/enoxaparin NOT indicated, tPA not for TIA; antiplatelets (aspirin, P2Y12 blockers) for secondary prevention.Events lasting hours then resolving are usually strokes (confirm on MRI)⭐ TIA = no infarction; never ignore — 3-4% progress to stroke

Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)Bleeding from a small deep vessel (same type as lacunes); subcortical — basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem (pons), cerebellum; only ~10% cortical. Hypertension → microaneurysms of deep penetrating vessels. Others: AVM, trauma, tumors; risk ↑ with cocaine, heavy alcohol. Focal deficit + headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion (↑ICP); rapid downhill course.Immediate noncontrast CT (blood appears white); CT/MR angiography for aneurysm/AVM.↓ICP: raise head of bed, hyperventilation (acutely), osmotic diuresis, surgical evacuation; anticonvulsants; antihypertensives; definitive aneurysm treatment if present. No anticoagulation or aspirin; BP control prevents rebleeds.Headache + vomiting + depressed consciousness⭐ Hypertensive ICH = deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum); no antithrombotics, lower ICP and BP

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)Bleeding between arachnoid & pia; usually traumatic or ruptured saccular aneurysm (also AVM). Worst headache ever, stiff neck, vomiting, no fever; usually nonfocal (except aneurysm near CN III → ptosis, eye down & out, dilated pupil). Mortality 40-50%.Noncontrast CT first (positive ~6 h). If suspicion high & CT normal → LP: high opening pressure, RBCs not decreasing tube 1→4, xanthochromia (even > 12 h).ICU, bedrest, analgesia, pneumatic compression stockings, stop antithrombotics; BP lowering ↓ rebleed but may ↑ infarction; early surgery — clipping or endovascular coiling; nimodipine (CCB) for vasospasm.Complications: hydrocephalus/↑ICP, vasospasm, rebleed⭐ SAH: worst headache ever → noncontrast CT; if normal → LP for xanthochromia; nimodipine prevents vasospasm

Cerebral aneurysm (saccular vs fusiform)Outward bulge of a weak vessel wall; 1% of population at autopsy, mostly asymptomatic until rupture. Saccular (berry) outpouching — much more likely to rupture; fusiform = diffuse widening. Sites: circle of Willis — AComm, PComm, MCA trifurcation (no supportive media). Risk: HTN (No. 1), smoking, fibromuscular dysplasia, ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos.CT or MR angiography in any suspected hemorrhagic stroke.Open surgical clipping or endoscopic coiling.PComm aneurysm → CN III compression⭐ Berry aneurysms: circle of Willis (AComm most often); associated with ADPKD & Ehlers-Danlos

History & exam in suspected strokeHPI: acute onset, motor/sensory/speech/special senses/CN/behavior; pattern of deficit (F A > L, F = A = L, L > F A); timing & progression. Accompanying: headache (hemorrhage), vomiting (hemorrhage or vertebrobasilar), vertigo (vertebrobasilar). BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time.Vitals: BP, pulse rate & rhythm (AF?). CV: carotid bruits, CHF, murmurs, apical impulse (LVH). Neuro: motor, sensory, CN, cerebellar, mental status, speech.—Irregularly irregular pulse = AF = embolic source⭐ Pattern of deficit (FA>L vs L>FA vs F=A=L) + accompanying symptoms localize the lesion

APP → amyloid plaque

  1. APPNeuronal transmembrane protein (chr 21), degraded by α-, β- and γ-secretases
  2. Aβ peptideNormal product of degradation (Aβ40); presenilin (γ-secretase) mutations → longer Aβ42/43
  3. OligomersExcess or mutant monomers → oligomers (some insoluble, toxic) → aggregates → fibrils
  4. PlaqueExtracellular amyloid accumulation → amyloid plaques
  5. DownstreamKinase activation → tau hyperphosphorylation; microglial activation & neuroinflammation; abnormal signaling; neuronal death

Tau → neurofibrillary tangle

  1. Hyperphosphorylationβ-amyloid activates kinases → tau hyperphosphorylated
  2. OligomersHyperphosphorylated tau oligomers form and accumulate
  3. PHFsOligomers aggregate into paired helical filaments
  4. NFTsPHFs aggregate into neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons
  5. DeathAffected neurons die → NFTs appear in the extracellular space

Neurodegenerative & dementiaMajor Neurocognitive Disorders — The Dementias (Major Neurocognitive Disorders lecture; drugs from NCD workshop) [Neurocognitive, Neurodegenerative & Development · Neurology / Psychiatry]· 18One row per neurocognitive disorder / dementia type — core features / DSM-5 criteria · onset & course · key differentiator (pathology, imaging) · treatment

Questions to answer for every dementia case

  1. 1 · Fits the definition?DSM-IV memory + 1 cognitive problem; DSM-5 ≥1 of 6 domains
  2. 2 · Course?Fast to several years (2-20) → FTD; intermittently progressive → multi-infarct; slowly progressive → AD, Binswanger; stable → NPH, traumatic
  3. 3 · Predominant symptoms?Memory → AD (vascular later); behaviour → FTD; parkinsonism → LBD, PDD; gait/bladder → NPH
  4. Age at onset?Older (>65) → AD; early onset with behaviour problems → FTD
  5. Family history?AD, FTD, CADASIL (rarely DLB)
  6. Discrete episodes / risk factors?Stepwise events + HTN, DM, CAD, PVD → vascular dementia

Alzheimer drug classes (from NCD workshop)

  1. Cholinesterase inhibitorsDonepezil (mild-severe AD; CYP2D6/3A4), rivastigmine (AChE + BuChE; transdermal patch; esterases — no CYP interactions; only ChEI for PDD), galantamine (competitive). AEs: N/D, bradycardia/syncope/falls, sleep disturbance; caution conduction disease, ulcer, asthma/COPD, seizures, BPH
  2. NMDA antagonistMemantine — moderate-severe AD, combined with ChEI in advanced AD, off-label vascular dementia; renal excretion ↓ by alkaline urine; AEs dizziness, confusion, agitation
  3. Anti-amyloid antibodiesLecanemab, donanemab — IV infusion; disease-modifying, modest; MCI/mild dementia + proven amyloid; ARIA (edema, microhemorrhage; APOE ε4)
  4. Avoid in elderlyBenzodiazepines, hypnotics, H1 antagonists, TCAs, antimuscarinics; antipsychotics ↑ death

Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) — definitionDSM-5: significant acquired decline in ≥1 of 6 cognitive domains — learning & memory, language, executive function, perceptual-motor, complex attention, social cognition; deficits interfere with independence in everyday activities; not exclusively during delirium; not better explained by another mental disorder (MDD, schizophrenia). DSM-IV 'dementia' = memory + 1 (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, executive dysfunction)5-8% at 65, doubling every 5 years; ~50% of >85 y; >55 million worldwide, ~10 million new cases/yr; usually gradual with death in 5-10 yearsCommon in the elderly but not a normal part of aging. vs mild NCD/MCI (function preserved); vs delirium (acute, fluctuating attention); vs depression (pseudodementia)History (from family/witnesses), MSE in every patient, physical exam (usually nonlocalizing), work-up for reversible causes⭐ Major NCD (DSM-5): decline in ≥1 of 6 cognitive domains that interferes with independence and is not only during delirium

MSE mnemonic ASEPTIC: Appearance, Speech, Emotion (mood/affect), Perception, Thought, Insight, Cognition. Alzheimer disease (major NCD due to AD)DSM-5: insidious onset, gradual progression in ≥2 domains; clear decline in memory & learning + ≥1 other domain; steady decline without long plateaus; no mixed etiology — or a causative AD gene mutation (family history/testing). Early: short-term memory loss (can't find keys; storage deficit, not helped by cues), long-term intact; middle/late: long-term memory lost, gait difficulty, seizures, sensory abnormalities, behaviour change (depression, apathy, agitation, wandering, disinhibition); executive deficits subtle → prominentMost common (>60%); risk rises after 65; slowly progressive, ~10 years from diagnosis to deathPathology: extracellular amyloid β plaques, neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau), cortical atrophy/widened sulci, compensatory ventricular enlargement; low ACh, excess glutamate. Negative work-up. Memory early, executive/focal/gait late. Down syndrome → early AD; logopenic PPA = AD pathologyCholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil mild-severe; rivastigmine & galantamine mild-moderate); memantine (NMDA antagonist) moderate-severe, combined in advanced AD; lecanemab/donanemab (IV anti-amyloid; MCI/mild, amyloid-positive; ARIA esp. APOE ε4); vitamin E modest functional benefit; NSAIDs, estrogen, ginkgo no benefit; avoid benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, antipsychotics (↑ death)⭐ AD: insidious, steadily progressive memory loss first; plaques (Aβ) + tangles (tau); low ACh, excess glutamate → ChEIs and memantine

Vascular dementia (major vascular NCD)DSM-5: onset temporally related to ≥1 cerebrovascular event OR decline prominent in complex attention (processing speed) & frontal-executive function; history/exam/imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease sufficient to explain the deficits. Heterogeneous: large-artery (usually cortical) infarcts, small-artery lacunes (basal ganglia, caudate, thalamus, internal capsule, cerebellum, brainstem), chronic periventricular white-matter ischemia (Binswanger)>15%; onset abrupt or insidious; course stepwise/fluctuating (multi-infarct) or continuously worsening (Binswanger)Atherosclerotic risk factors (DM, HTN, CAD, PVD); discrete episodes of deterioration; memory impairment later; early executive dysfunction, focal deficits, early gait abnormality; may have cognitive disability long before meeting dementia criteriaControl vascular risk factors; ChEIs also used; memantine off-label (blocks ischemia-induced NMDA excitotoxicity)⭐ Vascular dementia: abrupt/stepwise decline with early executive dysfunction, focal signs and vascular risk factors

Dementia first (before/with parkinsonism) = LBD vs parkinsonism >1 year before dementia = PDD. Small minority familialChEIs; avoid antipsychotics (severe sensitivity)⭐ LBD: fluctuating cognition + well-formed visual hallucinations + REM sleep behaviour disorder + parkinsonism; severe antipsychotic sensitivity
