Frontotemporal dementia — behavioural variant (bvFTD)Progressive behaviour/personality decline: apathy, reduced initiative, disinhibition, impulsivity, distractibility, hyperorality (overeating), hypersexuality, loss of social comportment, witzelsucht (fatuous humour), stereotyped/perseverative behaviour, social withdrawal; memory generally intact early. Frontal release of primitive reflexes: Babinski, glabellar, palmomental, snout~2%; young onset 50-65 (even 40s) — as common as early-onset AD in that group; course varies from rapid 1-2 years to many years (2-20); ½ have a first-degree family historyBehaviour > memory early (later withdrawn, aphasic, memory worse than behaviour); often misdiagnosed as a personality or late-onset psychiatric disorder; work-up negative. Pathology: asymmetric frontal & temporal atrophy, knife-edge gyri, neuronal loss in outer 3 cortical layersNo disease-specific treatment covered — clinical diagnosis, supportive/behavioural care⭐ bvFTD: age 50-65 with early personality change (disinhibition, hyperorality, apathy) and spared memory; knife-edge frontotemporal atrophy

Dementia differential & reversible causesWilson, Huntington, vitamin B12 & B1 deficiency, Addison, hypercalcemia, drug intoxication, heavy metals, brain trauma, paraneoplastic, Creutzfeldt-Jakob, HIV (HAND/HAD), neurosyphilis, SSPE, lipid storage diseases & leukodystrophies, pseudodementiaTransient: delirium, depression, transient global amnesia, syncope. Neurodegenerative & dementiaDelirium, Acute Confusional States & Wernicke-Korsakoff (Workshop: Major Neurocognitive Disorders and Acute Confusional States) [Neurocognitive, Neurodegenerative & Development · Neurology / Psychiatry]· 8One row per acute confusional / toxic-metabolic disorder — core features / DSM-5 criteria · onset & course · key differentiator · management

Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) for delirium

  1. 1 · Acute onset & fluctuating courseFrom family/nurse: acute change from baseline? Behaviour comes and goes during the day?
  2. 2 · InattentionEasily distractible, can't keep track of conversation
  3. 3 · Disorganized thinkingRambling, irrelevant, illogical, switching subjects
  4. 4 · Altered level of consciousnessAnything but 'alert': vigilant, lethargic, stupor, coma
  5. DiagnosisDelirium = features 1 + 2 + (3 or 4)
Fusion Session - Workshop - Major Nuerocognitive Disorders and Acute Confusional States - Fusion PDF
p.7

Work-up & management of acute confusion

  1. HistoryAcute? Altered consciousness? MOVESTUPID causes, new medications, intoxication/withdrawal, sleep-wake change, fluctuation, autonomic signs (sweating, tachycardia), PMH
  2. Re-examineRepeat the physical even if recently done; hunt for occult UTI and pneumonia (may lack fever/cough)
  3. InvestigationsCMP (glucose, Ca, electrolytes, LFTs, BUN, creatinine), CBC, UA + culture, toxicology screen, ethanol level, blood gases; ESR, Mg, ammonia, TSH/T3/T4, B12; chest x-ray, CT/MRI; LP last resort if meningitis suspected
  4. SafetyPad side rails, glove hands; restraints only as last resort
  5. Treat cause(s)No specific delirium treatment; there may be >1 cause (UTI + dehydration, pneumonia + DKA)
  6. Don't add toxicityAvoid sedatives, anxiolytics, antipsychotics

Why thiamine before glucose (Wernicke)

  1. Thiamine neededPyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) requires thiamine
  2. Glucose load↑ glucose metabolism consumes the remaining thiamine
  3. Lactic acidosisBlocked PDH → lactate accumulates (consider thiamine deficiency in unexplained lactic acidosis)
  4. Focal damageMammillary bodies & posteromedial thalamus; NMDA-mediated apoptotic cell death
  5. RuleGive IV thiamine first, then glucose; never delay for tests or imaging

Delirium / acute confusional state (acute toxic-metabolic encephalopathy)Transient global cerebral dysfunction without primary structural brain disease. DSM-5: (1) disturbed attention & awareness; (2) acute onset (hours-days), change from baseline, fluctuates during the day; (3) additional cognitive disturbance (memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial, perception); (4) not explained by an existing NCD, not in coma; (5) evidence of a medical condition, substance intoxication/withdrawal or medication cause. Also psychomotor hypo/hyperactivity with sympathetic overactivity, sleep-wake disturbance, fear/depression/euphoria/perplexityOnset hours-days; most remit when the cause is corrected. CAM: 1 acute onset & fluctuating + 2 inattention + either 3 disorganized thinking or 4 altered level of consciousnessA syndrome, not a disease — find the cause: MOVESTUPID (Metabolic, Oxygen, Vascular, Endocrine, Seizure/post-ictal, Trauma/Tumour, Uremia, Psychiatric, Infection, Drugs incl. alcohol intoxication/withdrawal). RAS dysfunction via cerebral edema, drug-induced neurotransmitter disruption (DA, ACh, glutamate, GABA, 5-HT), electrolytes, nutrition, toxins (CO, cyanide). Elderly: occult UTI or pneumonia (may lack fever, dysuria, cough); newly added drugs are likely culprits; aging ↑ susceptibilityNo specific treatment — full work-up, treat the underlying cause(s) (may be >1); safety: pad rails, glove hands, restraints only as last resort; don't add sedatives, anxiolytics or antipsychotics; avoid benzodiazepines, hypnotics, H1 antagonists, TCAs, antimuscarinics in the elderly⭐ Delirium = acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention/consciousness due to a medical cause (CAM: 1 + 2 + 3 or 4); treat the cause, avoid sedatives

Wernicke encephalopathyAcute neurologic emergency from thiamine (B1) deficiency: encephalopathy (confusion, disorientation, indifference, inattentiveness), ocular abnormalities — most commonly nystagmus (also lateral rectus/CN VI palsy, conjugate gaze palsy, sluggish pupils, ptosis, scotomata, anisocoria), ataxia (gait & stance)Acute; untreated → coma and death. MRI: mammillary body atrophy (~80% of chronic drinkers with WE; detectable within 1 week)Causes: chronic heavy alcohol use; also anorexia/psychiatric poor intake, hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged IV feeding, starvation, bariatric/GI surgery, malignancy, transplant, dialysis, AIDS, genetic. No diagnostic lab — normal serum thiamine doesn't exclude WE; imaging must not delay treatment. Glucose before thiamine → ↑ thiamine use (pyruvate dehydrogenase) → lactic acidosis → damage to mammillary bodies & posteromedial thalamus (NMDA excitotoxicity)IV thiamine BEFORE glucose — reverses most acute symptoms; don't wait for tests; thiamine in every alcohol detox⭐ Wernicke = confusion + ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus most common) + ataxia; give IV thiamine before glucose

Korsakoff syndrome (Korsakoff psychosis)Chronic late neuropsychiatric sequel of untreated WE: striking anterograde (+ retrograde) amnesia — can't form new memories; confabulation (involuntary plausible fabricated stories filling memory gaps — not lying); disorientation; possible visual/auditory hallucinations; polyneuritisChronic, permanent; risk rises with earlier drinking onset and greater amount/durationIrreversible mammillary body damage/infarction (amnesia); follows WE ('wet brain'); a static cause of persistent cognitive impairmentPrevention — treat WE with thiamine; abstinence⭐ Korsakoff = permanent anterograde amnesia + confabulation after untreated Wernicke (mammillary bodies)

COMPARE — delirium vs dementia vs psychotic disorder vs depressionDelirium: fluctuating consciousness, ↓ attention. Dementia: memory or other cognitive-domain impairment. Psychotic: deficits in reality testing. Depression: sadness, loss of interest/pleasure (SIGECAPS)Delirium: acute, remits when cause corrected. Dementia: chronic, slow onset, progressive. Psychotic: usually slow onset with prodrome, chronic with exacerbations. Depression: single or recurrent episodes, may be chronicAssociated: delirium — disorientation, visual hallucinations, agitation or apathy, withdrawal, memory/attention impairment; dementia — disorientation, agitation; psychotic — social withdrawal, apathy. Only delirium impairs level of consciousness/attention; dementia can't be diagnosed if deficits occur only during deliriumDelirium → find & treat cause · dementia → work-up, ChEIs · depression → treat (reversible 'pseudodementia')⭐ Acute + fluctuating attention/consciousness = delirium; chronic progressive memory loss with clear consciousness = dementia

COMPARE — Wernicke vs KorsakoffWE: confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia. KS: anterograde + retrograde amnesia, confabulationWE acute and largely reversible with thiamine; KS chronic and permanentSame cause (thiamine deficiency, usually alcohol) and site (mammillary bodies); KS follows untreated WEWE: emergency IV thiamine before glucose · KS: prevention⭐ Wernicke is the reversible acute stage; Korsakoff the permanent amnestic stage

Epilepsy & seizuresSeizures & epilepsy (TBL: Epilepsy and Syncope, Part 1) [Epilepsy · Clinical]· 37FORMAT — one row per seizure type / topic: features → EEG & work-up → localization or cause → the feature that separates it from its look-alikes

Phases of a seizure

  1. ProdromeBefore the seizure
  2. Stage 1 — AuraBeginning of the seizure activity; a focal seizure the patient can describe
  3. Stage 2 — Middle (ictal)During the seizure
  4. Stage 3 — Ending (post-ictal)After the seizure; borders of ictal, interictal and post-ictal are often indistinct
Fusion Session - TBL - Epilepsy and Syncope - Anti-Epileptics- Session PDFp.9Fusion Session - TBL - Epilepsy and Syncope - Anti-Epileptics- Session PDFp.12
1 / 2

Clinical approach to a seizure

  1. HistoryCollect information from the patient and witnesses; use clinical reasoning to classify the seizure; consider reversible causes
  2. Physical examNeurological exam and injuries; fundoscopy (CNS lesion); stigmata of Sturge-Weber, tuberous sclerosis, Chédiak-Higashi
  3. InvestigationsBy etiology: CBC, electrolytes, glucose, toxicology, LP/CSF if infection suspected; EEG if epilepsy suspected (24-h EEG ↑ yield; normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy)
  4. ImagingMRI is the image of choice; CT if stroke or intracranial hemorrhage is suspected
  5. ManagementDepends on the type. During a tonic-clonic seizure: do not try to stop the movements, put nothing in the mouth; drugs per pharmacology

Status epilepticus — timeline

  1. Old definitionSingle seizure > 30 min, or a series without regaining function between seizures over 30 min
  2. Operational definition≥ 5 min of continuous seizures, or ≥ 2 discrete seizures with incomplete recovery of consciousness between them
  3. ≤ 5 minInitiate drug therapy within 5 minutes of seizure onset
  4. > 30 minBrain damage possible; poor outcome and risk of death

COMPARE — Seizure vs epilepsySeizure: sudden change in behavior caused by electrical hypersynchronization of neuronal networks in the cerebral cortex. Epilepsy: a disease with lasting derangement of brain function and predisposition to recurring seizuresAn interictal (between-seizure) discharge on EEG can establish epilepsy after one seizureAbnormal bursts of hyper-synchronous activity from cortical neuronsEpilepsy = ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 h apart OR 1 unprovoked seizure + interictal EEG discharge. A seizure is not epilepsy⭐ Epilepsy = 2 unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or 1 + interictal discharge

EEG basicsScalp electrodes (glue/paste, painless) record brain electrical activity; abnormal bursts appear as 'spikes' and/or 'waves' of increased voltageA spike discharge is not itself a clinical seizure — it must propagate. EEG only picks up large, superficial bursts; a normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy; 24-hour EEG increases yieldConvexity focus → discharges in a limited region; deep focus (mesial temporal) → EEG may be normalBursts are common in normal (young) brains and self-extinguish; seizures occur only when they spread⭐ Normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy (deep foci, small bursts)

Causes — VITAMINSVascular (hematoma, stroke); Infectious (meningitis, encephalitis, abscess, AIDS); Trauma (head injury); Autoimmune / AV malformations, congenital malformations; Metabolic (electrolytes — hypoglycemia, hypoxia, hypotension, hyperthermia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia; hyper/hypoglycemia; drugs, alcohol, withdrawal; uremia); Idiopathic; Neoplasm (tumors, metastases); Structural (congenital, acquired)Choose investigations by etiologyMechanisms: (I) decreased inhibition, (II) defective activation of GABA neurons, (III) increased activation (reorganized excitatory circuits after brain injury); genetic or acquired channelopathiesAEDs act by blocking propagation (ion channels / neurotransmitters). Age is related to the cause⭐ VITAMINS: Vascular, Infectious, Trauma, Autoimmune/AVM, Metabolic, Idiopathic, Neoplasm, Structural

Causes by ageNeonatal (<1 mo): perinatal hypoxia/ischemia, intracranial hemorrhage/trauma, CNS infection, metabolic, drug withdrawal, developmental, genetic. Infant/child (1 mo–12 y): febrile seizures, genetic, CNS infection, developmental, trauma, idiopathic. Adolescent (12–18 y): trauma, genetic, infection, tumor, illicit drugs, idiopathicWork-up guided by the likely cause for ageYoung adult (18–35 y): trauma, alcohol withdrawal, illicit drugs, brain tumor, idiopathic. Older adult (>35 y): cerebrovascular disease, brain tumor, alcohol withdrawal, metabolic (uremia, hepatic failure, electrolytes, glucose), Alzheimer's and other degenerative diseases, idiopathicChild → febrile; young adult → trauma/alcohol/drugs; >35 → stroke/tumor⭐ New seizure >35 y: think cerebrovascular disease or tumor

Classification (ILAE 2017)Onset: focal (one part of cortex, previously 'partial'), generalized (entire cortex simultaneously, loss of consciousness) or unknown. Focal → aware or impaired awareness; each onset → motor or non-motor. Focal motor: automatisms, atonic, clonic, epileptic spasms, hyperkinetic, myoclonic, tonic; focal non-motor: autonomic, behavior arrest, cognitive, emotional, sensory. Generalized motor: tonic-clonic, clonic, myoclonic, myoclonic-tonic-clonic, myoclonic-atonic, atonic, epileptic spasms; generalized non-motor = absence (typical, atypical, myoclonic, eyelid myoclonia)ILAE framework: seizure types → epilepsy types (focal, generalized, combined generalized & focal, unknown) → epilepsy syndromes; co-morbidities considered throughoutEtiology: genetic, structural, metabolic, immune, infectious, unknownFocal seizures can become secondarily generalized (spread subcortically, cross the midline, then whole cortex)⭐ Focal = one area (aware vs impaired); generalized = whole cortex at once

Focal aware seizure (simple partial / aura)Patient remains AWARE and can report symptoms: sensory, motor, autonomic or psychic without impaired cognition — paresthesia, shaking, flashing lights, hallucinations, lip smacking, odd sounds/smells, heart racing, rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, vertigo. Usually < 2 min. An aura is the beginning of the seizure — enough brain to cause symptoms but not to impair consciousnessEEG may show interictal spikes (poor sensitivity) or be normal if deep; ambulatory EEG if frequent; MRI may show a structural lesionSymptoms depend on the cortical region where the activity arises (see cortex row). Case 7: 6 yo with ~1-min episodes of not seeing clearly, fully aware, difficult birth, abnormal EEG → most likely focal aware seizure / focal epilepsy (answer not given)Aura described by the patient localizes the focus; may progress to focal impaired or generalized⭐ Aware, can describe it, < 2 min = focal aware; the aura IS the seizure

Focal motor/sensory seizure — cortex → symptomMotor cortex: twitching of the contralateral hand → clonic or tonic contralateral limbs. Somatosensory cortex: contralateral paresthesias. Auditory cortex: voices, music, roaring. Visual cortex: flashes of light, hallucinationsEEG over the corresponding convexityCase 1/2: 7 yo, twitching of the right face and oral cavity every 5 min, no LOC → simple partial (focal aware motor) seizure; focus most likely the lateral aspect of the left frontal (precentral) gyrus — face area (answer not given)Symptom side is contralateral to the active cortex⭐ Right face twitching = left lateral motor cortex (face area)

Focal impaired awareness seizure (complex partial)Altered mental status but not total loss of consciousness; cannot respond appropriately; impaired recollection. May start with an aura, then behavioral arrest (staring) and automatisms — chewing, lip smacking, swallowing, 'picking'. Duration 60–90 s; post-ictal confusion (seconds to an hour)EEG may be normal (mesial temporal focus is far from scalp electrodes)Frequently mesial temporal lobe, limbic system, frontal regions → bizarre behaviors, emotional outbursts, psychiatric symptoms. Case 4: 25 yo, unaware 'funny turns', staring, yawning, picking at clothes >1 min, drowsy after → focal impaired awareness (answer not given)Staring + automatisms + post-ictal confusion, but not unconscious⭐ Staring + lip smacking/picking + amnesia for event = complex partial (temporal lobe)

COMPARE — Temporal vs frontal lobe seizuresTemporal: rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, olfactory and auditory hallucination, automatisms (fidgeting with hands, chewing, lip smacking). COMPARE — Mesial vs lateral (neocortical) temporal lobe epilepsyMesial: aura visceral, gustatory, autonomic; autonomic phenomena; motionless stare + automatism; history of febrile seizures; duration > 2 min. Lateral: aura auditory hallucinations and illusions; no autonomic phenomena; same stare/automatism; no febrile history; shorterMRI (coronal T2): atrophy of the hippocampus, fornix and mammillary body, enlarged temporal horn = mesial temporal sclerosisMesial temporal lobe = amygdala, hippocampus, uncus, dentate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus; MTLE often begins in the hippocampus, ~80% of temporal lobe seizures; onset ~age 10–20 after febrile seizure or early brain injuryFebrile seizure history + visceral aura = mesial; auditory aura = lateral⭐ MTLE = ~80% of temporal lobe seizures; hippocampal sclerosis, prior febrile seizures

Status epilepticusHistorically a single seizure > 30 min, or a series without regaining function between seizures over 30 min. Operational definition: ≥5 min of continuous seizures or ≥2 discrete seizures with incomplete recovery of consciousness between themDo not wait for 30 min — treat once seizures continue for more than a few minutesProlonged > 30 min → brain damage possible; poor outcome and risk of deathStart drug therapy within 5 minutes of seizure onset (drugs: Part 2 / pharmacology)⭐ Status = ≥5 min or ≥2 seizures without recovery; treat within 5 min

Criteria: convulsion with temperature > 38 °C (100.4 °F); age > 6 mo and < 5 y; no CNS infection/inflammation; no acute systemic metabolic abnormality; no previous afebrile seizuresExclude CNS infection and metabolic causesCauses: infections — especially HHV-6 (roseola, sixth disease); immunizations (esp. MMR — fever 8–14 days after); family history increases riskNot a form of epilepsy; excluded if the child has had a previous non-febrile seizure⭐ Febrile seizures (6 mo–5 y, > 38 °C, no CNS infection) are not epilepsy

COMPARE — Syncope vs seizureSyncope: slower onset; dysautonomic prodrome — warmth, nausea, light-headedness, sweating, cold hands, palpitations, pallor; transient LOC with loss of postural tone; myoclonic jerks or tonic posturing may occur (esp. if kept upright); 1–2 min. Rapid recovery with recumbence; no post-ictal confusion, drowsiness or amnesia; can recall prodromeSyncope: ECG (ambulatory if arrhythmia suspected), echocardiography, orthostatic BP. Seizure: EEG, MRISyncope = interrupted cerebral blood flow/hypoxia, orthostatic hypotension, vaso-vagal, shallow-water blackout. A few clonic jerks while 'out' come from hypoxic hyperexcitability — not epilepsyGeneralized seizure: sudden, no warning, complete amnesia, urinary incontinence, post-ictal confusion; syncope: prodrome + quick recovery lying flat⭐ Prodrome + pallor + rapid recovery lying down, no post-ictal confusion = syncope

DisorderCore features / DSM-5-TR criteriaDuration · thresholdKey differentiatorTreatment⭐ Will Be TestedImage
Depressive disorders — overview & epidemiologyPersistent sad, empty, or irritable mood + changes that significantly impair daily functioning. Members: MDD, persistent depressive disorder, DMDD, PMDD, substance/medication-induced, due to another medical condition, other specified, unspecified. Distinguished by duration, timing and presumed etiology.US lifetime MDD 17% (double developing countries); females 2×. White 18% vs Black 10% (but more chronic/impairing in Black Americans). 12-mo MDD 10.4% (18–34 y) vs 2.6% (>65 y); 11.5% older hospital pts, 13.5% home-health recipientsDepression declines with age, but medically ill older adults are at ↑ riskPharmacologic + psychotherapy (see treatment rows)⭐ All depressive disorders = persistent sad/empty/irritable mood that impairs daily functioning; they differ by duration, timing, etiology

Major depressive disorder (MDD)Depressed mood OR loss of interest/pleasure + total ≥ 5 of 9 symptoms (SIG E CAPS): Sleep ↑/↓, Interest ↓, Guilt/worthlessness, Energy ↓, Concentration ↓, Appetite/weight change, Psychomotor agitation/retardation, Suicidal ideation. Irritable mood can replace depressed mood in children. Change from prior functioning; clinically significant distress/impairment; not due to substance/medical condition. Across cultures, somatic complaints (insomnia, fatigue) often the presenting complaint; often missed in primary care≥ 2 weeks; ≥ 5 symptoms (≥ 1 = depressed mood or anhedonia)vs PDD: shorter (2 wk vs 2 y) but more symptoms (5 vs 2). Still diagnosed after bereavement if criteria metFirst line SSRI (fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline); CBT + antidepressant > either alone; exercise; ECT if urgent; TMS. Response expected by 4–6 wk follow-up⭐ MDD = depressed mood or anhedonia + ≥5 SIG E CAPS symptoms for ≥2 weeks

Persistent depressive disorder (PDD, dysthymia)Depressed mood most of the day, more days than not + ≥ 2 of: poor appetite/overeating, insomnia/hypersomnia, low energy/fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration/indecision, hopelessness. Not substance/medical; clinically significant distress/impairment≥ 2 years adults (≥ 1 year children/adolescents, mood may be irritable); no more than 2 symptom-free months in 1 yearLonger duration but lower symptom count than MDDAntidepressants + psychotherapy (as for depressive disorders)⭐ PDD needs only 2 symptoms but for ≥2 years (≥1 year in children)

Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD)Childhood diagnosis, much more common in males. Severe recurrent temper outbursts (verbal/physical, out of proportion, inconsistent with developmental level) + irritable/angry mood between outbursts most of the day. Not substance/medicalOutbursts ≥ 3×/week; symptoms ≥ 12 months (symptom-free ≤ 3 months); ≥ 2 settings (home, school, peers); onset usually < 10 y; first diagnosis only between age 6 and 18Angry ALL the time (not just tantrums). In children, chronic irritability → DMDD rather than bipolar disorderNot specified in lecture⭐ DMDD: outbursts ≥3×/week + persistently irritable mood between them, ≥12 months, diagnosed age 6–18

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)Behavioral/mood symptoms present in most cycles, severe enough to interfere with functioning. ≥ 1 core: hopelessness/depressed mood/self-critical thoughts; tension/anxiety; sudden sadness/rejection sensitivity; anger/irritability. Plus others (↓ interest, poor concentration, fatigue, appetite change/cravings, sleep change, overwhelmed, breast tenderness/bloating/weight gain/aches)Total ≥ 5 symptoms; begin the week before menses, end within first few days of mensesTiming tied to menstrual cycleNot specified in lecture⭐ PMDD symptoms start the week before menstruation and end within the first few days of menses

Substance/medication-induced depressive disorderDepressed mood or anhedonia developing soon after intoxication/withdrawal or medication exposure. Culprits: alcohol, opiates, cocaine, amphetamines, corticosteroids; also common meds — β blockers, birth control, PPIs, benzodiazepines. Not better explained by another depressive disorder; not exclusively during deliriumOnset soon after exposure; disturbance does not persist long (e.g., > 1 month) after exposure/withdrawalTemporal link to substance; albuterol (β agonist) is NOT associated with depressionRemove offending agent; always ask about drug use⭐ Always ask about drugs — β blockers, birth control, PPIs and benzodiazepines can cause depression

Specifiers — with peripartum onset · with seasonal patternPeripartum onset: major depressive episode begins in pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery; with or without psychotic features. Seasonal pattern (recurrent MDD): episodes related to time of year; remission or mania/hypomania also seasonal; seasonal episodes outnumber nonseasonal over lifetimePeripartum: pregnancy → 4 wk postpartum. Seasonal: 2 seasonal MDEs in last 2 y, no nonseasonal onesSpecifiers are added to a depressive diagnosis, not stand-alone disordersPostpartum MDD: antidepressants OK even while breastfeeding (benefit > low infant risk) + psychotherapy⭐ 'With peripartum onset' = episode during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery

Pathogenesis: circadian rhythm changes affecting serotoninRegular seasonal recurrenceSeasonal timing of episodesAntidepressants, light therapy, psychotherapy; sleep hygiene, daily outdoor activity⭐ SAD = circadian change affecting serotonin; treat with light therapy, antidepressants, psychotherapy

COMPARE — Normal grief vs major depressive episodeGrief: predominant affect = emptiness and loss; mixture of sadness and pleasant emotions; pain in waves or pangs; preoccupied with thoughts/memories of the deceased; hopeful and consolable. MDE: persistent depressed mood, inability to anticipate pleasure; continuous gloom/despair; self-critical, pessimistic ruminations; rarely consolableMDD criteria (≥ 5 symptoms, ≥ 2 wk) can still be met within a year of a deathUncharacteristic of grief: guilt unrelated to deceased, thoughts of death, worthlessness, psychomotor slowing, functional impairment, hallucinations (with exceptions)Grief: support. MDD: treat as MDD even after bereavement⭐ Worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the deceased, psychomotor slowing and impairment point to MDD, not grief

Suicide risk factors (across disorders)Risk factors: male, single/living alone, hopelessness, substance use, firearm ownership; borderline PD ↑ future attempts. Bipolar: ~14× general population, ~25% of suicide deaths, more attempts than MDD (activation/impulsivity). Schizophrenia spectrum: young age, high IQ, higher SES, higher premorbid functioning; brief psychotic disorder ↑ risk during acute episode. BDD: high suicidal behavior; panic disorder ↑ suicidalityAntidepressant warning: children, adolescents, adults 18–24 during first 1–2 months of treatmentAsking about suicide does NOT increase riskAsk specifically; monitor after starting antidepressants; follow-up; suicide risk assessment in schizophrenia spectrum; ECT first line if high suicide risk⭐ Asking about suicide does not increase risk; antidepressant warning for ages ≤24 in the first 1–2 months

Causes & neurobiology of depressionGenetic + environmental + psychological. Childhood adversity (trauma, neglect, low support, parental divorce/death/mental illness); chronic/disabling medical illness. Imaging: ↑ ventricular-brain ratio, ↓ frontal lobe and hippocampal volume (also seen in at-risk adolescents → may precede illness); faster gray-matter pruning in depressed adolescents. Neurotransmitters: ↓ serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, ↓ GABA, ↑ glutamate (monoamine deficit)MZ concordance 37%; heritability women 42% vs men 29%Decreased (not increased) hippocampal volume; increased (not decreased) ventricular-brain ratioPharmacotherapy targets the ↓ monoamines⭐ Depression: ↓ hippocampal and frontal volume, ↑ ventricular-brain ratio, ↓ 5-HT/NE/DA/GABA, ↑ glutamate

Neurotransmitter–disorder table (Table 1)Norepinephrine: ↑ anxiety, ↓ depression. Dopamine: ↑ schizophrenia, ↓ Parkinson disease and depression. Serotonin: ↓ anxiety and depression. Acetylcholine: ↓ Alzheimer, ↓ Huntington, ↓ during REM sleep. GABA: ↓ anxiety and Huntington—Anxiety = ↑ NE but ↓ 5-HT and ↓ GABA; stress/anxiety lecture lists 5-HT, GABA, NE—⭐ Dopamine ↑ in schizophrenia, ↓ in Parkinson & depression; GABA ↓ in anxiety & Huntington

Selected theories of depressionBiological: heredity, altered neurotransmitters, limbic-HPA axis abnormalities. Learned helplessness: repeated failed attempts to control events → hopelessness, apathy. Psychosocial: loss of primary attachment figure, low self-esteem, negative interpretation of life events; accumulated stressors. ACE study (CDC/Kaiser, 9,508 respondents; 7 categories of abuse/household dysfunction): > 50% ≥ 1 category, 25% > 2≥ 4 ACE categories → 4–12× risk of alcohol/substance use, depression, suicide attempts; 2–4× smoking, poor health, STDs; 1.4–1.6× inactivity, severe obesityGraded (dose-response) relationship between ACE count and adult disease (IHD, cancer, lung, liver disease, fractures)—⭐ ACE study: graded relationship — ≥4 categories gives 4–12× risk of depression, substance use, suicide attempts

Differential diagnosis & comorbidity of depressionIrritability/poor focus in children may be ADHD. Elderly → memory or somatic complaints (fatigue, ↓ appetite, weight loss). Part of bipolar disorder and cyclothymia; with hallucinations/delusions may be mistaken for schizophrenia. Medical mimics: cancer, TB, malabsorption. Comorbid: panic disorder, OCD, substance use, anorexia, bulimia, borderline PD—Always screen for prior mania/hypomania (bipolar) and medical causesThorough history, exam, psychiatric evaluation⭐ Elderly depressed patients present with memory issues or somatic complaints (fatigue, appetite/weight loss)

Depression in older adultsMost common psychiatric disorder in older adults but not a normal part of aging. Triggers: loss of spouse/support, ↓ social status, declining health. Presents with cognitive impairment (memory loss, slowed speech) = pseudodementia (a description, not a diagnosis; may be reversible) or somatic complaints. ↑ cardiac disease and post-MI death. Risk factors: female, single/divorced/widowed, low support, stressful events, chronic illness, insomniaScreen all > 60 y; nursing home/assisted living: 2 weeks after admission, then every 6 monthsTools: MMSE, Geriatric Depression Scale, Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia, MoCATreatable — missed depression = missed chance to improve quality of life⭐ Pseudodementia = cognitive decline in the elderly that looks like dementia but is due to depression

COMPARE — Depression (pseudodementia) vs dementiaPseudodementia: sudden onset, rapid progression, aware of and highlights deficits, appears depressed, anhedonia, "I don't know" answers, better in the evening. Dementia: gradual onset, slow decline, denies/unaware of deficits, not depressed, can feel pleasure, near-miss answers/confabulation, conceals difficulties, worse in the evening (sundowning)—"I don't know" + highlights deficits → depression; confabulation + conceals → dementiaDepression-related cognitive impairment may be reversible with treatment⭐ "I don't know" answers and patient highlighting deficits = pseudodementia; confabulation and concealing = dementia

Assessment of depressionVague physical complaints (poor concentration, low energy). Rule out medical causes (hypothyroidism, cancer, TB). Ask about medications/drugs. Ask specifically about suicidal thoughts or actions—Borderline PD ↑ risk of future suicide attemptsThorough medical history, exam, psychiatric evaluation⭐ Asking about suicide does not increase the risk of an attempt

Pharmacologic treatment of depressionSSRIs first line (fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline) — block 5-HT reuptake. SNRIs ↑ 5-HT + NE. TCAs ↑ 5-HT. MAOIs block breakdown of 5-HT, NE, DA and tyramine → tyramine foods (cheese, processed meat, pickled/smoked fish) → hypertensive crisis. Atypicals: mirtazapine (sedation + weight gain → insomnia/weight loss), trazodone (insomnia), bupropion (↓ seizure threshold; avoid in eating disorders)Hypertensive crisis = SBP > 180 or DBP > 120 mm Hg; follow-up 4–6 wkSSRIs may ↑ agitation/restlessness; trazodone sedates but no weight gainPostpartum: antidepressants + psychotherapy, OK when breastfeeding⭐ Depressed + insomnia + weight loss → mirtazapine (sedation and weight gain)

Non-pharmacologic treatment — CBT, exercise, ECT, TMSCBT: mood tied to thoughts; replace negative/inaccurate thoughts; addresses cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, future). Exercise improves symptoms. ECT = generalized seizure under anesthesia. TMS: as effective as medication, less than ECTECT first line when urgent: high suicide risk, malnutrition, dehydration, refusal to eat; also refractory depression and pregnancyECT gives rapid relief; CBT + SSRI takes weeksCBT + antidepressant > either alone⭐ Depressed patient refusing to eat or at high suicide risk → ECT (rapid; safe in pregnancy)

CBT — cognitive distortionsAll-or-nothing thinking; disqualifying the positive; automatic negative reactions; magnifying/minimizing; overgeneralization (broad conclusion from one event); personalization; mental filter (single negative detail); catastrophizing (worst conclusion, little evidence); compare and despair—Recognize and challenge self-defeating thought patternsCBT components: education, questioning thoughts, challenging beliefs, relaxation/exposure, coping/stress/assertiveness training, homework⭐ Catastrophizing = jumping to the worst possible conclusion with little evidence

COMPARE — Psychotherapies for depressionCBT: changes inaccurate thoughts + problematic behaviors. Interpersonal psychotherapy: grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits. Problem-solving therapy: rational problem-solving steps. Behavioral activation: behavioral component of CBT — ↓ withdrawal/avoidance, routines, pleasure/mastery. Family/couples: corrects distorted communication. Short-term psychodynamic: insight into repetitive conflicts, childhood parallels. Supportive: active listening, validation, reassurance, role modeling—Match therapy to problem (e.g., role dispute → IPT)Often combined with medication⭐ Interpersonal psychotherapy targets grief, role disputes, role transitions, interpersonal deficits

Bipolar & related disorders — overviewBridge between depressive and psychotic disorders (symptoms, family history, shared genetics). DSM-5-TR: bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic, substance-induced, due to another medical condition, not elsewhere classified. 'Manic-depressive' no longer used—Depressed-mood flowchart: rule out medical/drug causes, then look for any mania/hypomaniaMood stabilizers + psychotherapy⭐ Bipolar disorders overlap depressive and psychotic disorders in symptoms, family history and genetics

Manic episode (concept)Abnormally, persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood + ↑ goal-directed activity/energy, most of the day nearly every day. DIG FAST: Distractibility, Impulsivity/Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity/agitation, ↓ need for Sleep, Talkativeness/pressured speech. Psychotic features in ~⅔ (only during the episode), poor insight, uncharacteristic behavior (aggression, illegal acts, gambling, hypersexuality)> 1 week, or any duration if hospitalization needed; ≥ 3 symptoms (≥ 4 if only irritable)Marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis = mania (not hypomania)Diagnostic emergency (high-risk behavior)⭐ Mania = ≥1 week (any duration if hospitalized) + DIG FAST; a diagnostic emergency

Bipolar I disorderA single manic episode defines it (depressive episodes common but not required — usually precede/follow). Criterion B: ≥ 3 DIG FAST symptoms (≥ 4 if irritable). Marked social/occupational impairment OR hospitalization OR psychotic features (psychosis more common in BP than depressive disorders)Manic episode > 1 week (or any duration if hospitalized)Mania required; hypomanic & depressive episodes common but not requiredMood stabilizers; ECT first line if suicidal or refusing to eat/drink (safe in pregnancy); psychoeducation, ISRT, family therapy, CBT⭐ One manic episode is enough to diagnose bipolar I

Clinically significant distress/impairment; not better explained by another disorder, substance, or medical conditionHypomania ≥ 4 days; MDE ≥ 2 weeksAny manic episode → re-diagnose as bipolar IAs for bipolar disorders⭐ Bipolar II = hypomania + major depression, never mania

Antidepressant/ECT-emergent hypomaniaA full hypomanic episode during antidepressant or ECT treatment that persists beyond the physiological effect of treatment = sufficient evidence for a hypomanic episode. SSRIs (mixed evidence) may switch predisposed patients into hypomania/mania. Other triggers: antidepressants without mood stabilizer, appetite suppressants, stimulants, thyroid meds, corticosteroidsPersists after the drug effect wears offPersisting hypomania → evaluate for bipolar spectrumCareful monitoring when prescribing antidepressants⭐ Hypomania that persists beyond the antidepressant's effect counts toward a bipolar diagnosis

Cyclothymic disorderNumerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that never meet criteria for a hypomanic, manic, or major depressive episode; present ≥ half the time; distress/impairment. Milder than bipolar I/II≥ 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents); no symptom-free period > 2 monthsChronic, subthreshold swings — no full episodesMay require treatment to manage symptoms⭐ Cyclothymia: ≥2 years of subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms, never a full episode

Bipolar II: manic never; hypomanic + depressive episodes required. Causes of bipolar disorderGenetic + biological + social. Advanced paternal age (> 45 y → 6× risk vs 20–24 y). ↓ serotonin with ↑ glutamate and dopamine (glutamate, dopamine). MRI: disrupted white matter, gray-matter loss in prefrontal cortex → ↓ connections to amygdala; lower gray matter with longer illness. Environmental: childhood abuse/trauma, life stressors, substance abuse, hormonal changes (puberty, pregnancy, postpartum, menopause), medicationsFirst-degree relative 5–10%; MZ twins 40–70% vs DZ 5%MZ < 100% → environment also mattersPsychoeducation, stress management, medication management⭐ Bipolar: MZ concordance 40–70%; ↓ serotonin with ↑ glutamate and dopamine

Bipolar — suicide & comorbiditiesSuicide: ~14× general population; ~25% of all suicide deaths; more attempts than MDD. Medical comorbidities: migraine, pain, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity. Psychiatric: personality (borderline), ADHD, impulse-control, anxiety, eating, substance use disorders—Comorbidities complicate treatment and worsen outcomesEarly detection, mood stabilizers + psychotherapy, integrated treatment⭐ Bipolar disorder carries ~14× suicide risk and ~25% of suicide deaths

Bipolar — psychotherapy & non-medication treatmentCBT: improves adherence but not consistently shown to ↓ episodes. Interpersonal & social rhythm therapy (ISRT): developed for bipolar; stabilizes daily routines/sleep-wake (circadian) rhythms. Family therapy: communication, supportive environment. Group/individual psychoeducation: ↓ stigma, guilt, learned helplessness; group form ↓ mood episodes and hospitalizations—Group psychoeducation is the one shown to reduce episodes & hospitalizationECT: rapid; first line if suicidal or refusing to eat/drink; safe in pregnancy⭐ ISRT was developed specifically for bipolar disorder (stabilizes social/circadian rhythms)

Differential diagnosis of bipolar disorderMDD (no mania/hypomania); schizoaffective (psychosis + mood episodes); schizophrenia (psychosis without distinct mood episodes); other bipolar (I, cyclothymia); anxiety disorders; substance/medication-induced (intoxication/withdrawal); ADHD (impulsivity, inattention — esp. children); borderline PD (mood instability, impulsivity); childhood irritability → DMDD—Longitudinal pattern, family history, functional impairment—⭐ In children, chronic irritability is diagnosed as DMDD rather than bipolar disorder

PsychoticSchizophrenia Spectrum & Other Psychotic Disorders (TBL: Psychotic and Bipolar Disorders) [Psychiatry · Behavioral Science]· 17FORMAT — one row per DSM-5-TR disorder (core criteria → duration/threshold → how to tell it apart → treatment); COMPARE rows contrast look-alikes; concept rows hold stand-alone teaching points

Psychotic disorders — sort by time course

  1. 1 day – 1 month≥ 1 psychotic symptom → brief psychotic disorder
  2. 1 – 6 months≥ 2 symptoms → schizophreniform disorder
  3. ≥ 6 months (≥ 1 month active)≥ 2 symptoms, ≥ 1 positive → schizophrenia
  4. ≥ 1 month, delusions onlyfunctioning intact, hallucinations not prominent → delusional disorder
  5. Psychosis ≥ 2 wk without mood + mood for majority→ schizoaffective disorder

Psychosis — schizophrenia spectrum overviewPsychosis = thoughts/perceptions disturbed so the person cannot tell what is real. Spectrum: schizophrenia, schizoaffective, delusional, brief psychotic, schizophreniform. Symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms—Schizophrenia is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out schizoaffective, depressive/bipolar with psychotic features)Antipsychotics⭐ Schizophrenia is a diagnosis of exclusion

Delusions (concept)Fixed, false beliefs despite conflicting evidence. Types: erotomanic ("they love me"), grandiose, persecutory (most common), referential (ideas of reference), religious, somatic, nihilistic. Bizarre delusions (implausible, not understandable to same-culture peers): thought withdrawal, thought insertion, delusions of control—Persecutory = most common typeBuild trust without "going along with" the delusion⭐ Persecutory delusions are the most common; thought insertion/withdrawal/control are bizarre delusions

Hallucinations (concept)Sensory experience of something not present (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory). Psychotic disorders → auditory most common (voices; command hallucinations). Must occur with a clear sensorium—Tactile/visual → think organic; hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) are normalInvestigate organic causes⭐ Tactile and/or visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause and should be investigated

Disorganized thinking & catatonia (concept)Formal thought disorder (inferred from speech): derailment/loose associations (knight's move thinking); tangentiality (leaves topic, never returns — vs circumstantiality, which returns); incoherence/word salad. Grossly disorganized behavior (silliness → agitation). Catatonia: ↓ reactivity — negativism, posturing, stupor, mutism, catatonic excitement, stereotypy, echolalia, echopraxia, staring, grimacing—Catatonia occurs in psychotic, bipolar, depressive disorders and medical conditions → full exam—⭐ Tangentiality never returns to the point; circumstantiality eventually does

Negative symptoms (concept)Lack of normal function: diminished emotional expression (face, eye contact, prosody, gestures), avolition, alogia, anhedonia, asociality; flat affect, withdrawal, poor grooming; cognitive dysfunction (attention, memory)Often precede positive symptoms in slow-onset diseaseAssociated with worse prognosis; social withdrawal = negative symptomLifelong treatment often required⭐ Negative symptoms (avolition, alogia, anhedonia, asociality) predict a more severe prognosis

Schizophrenia≥ 2 of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms — ≥ 1 must be one of the first three; marked impairment in work, relationships, or self-care. Schizoaffective and mood disorder with psychotic features ruled out; not substance/medical. Most severe psychotic disorder. Comorbid: depression, anxiety, SUD, neurologic, metabolic syndrome (antipsychotic AEs)Active symptoms ≥ 1 month; total ≥ 6 monthsNo distinct mood episodes (vs schizoaffective/bipolar)Antipsychotics (D2 block in mesolimbic → ↓ positive sx), SGAs risperidone/olanzapine fewer AEs than FGA haloperidol; LAI IM q3–4 wk; family therapy ↓ relapse; case management⭐ Schizophrenia: ≥2 symptoms (≥1 delusions/hallucinations/disorganized speech) for ≥6 months incl. 1 month active

Schizophrenia — epidemiology, race & culture> 21 million worldwide; adult prevalence ~1%; children 0.04%. Onset males early–mid 20s, females late 20s; M:F 1.4:1. Mostly gradual onset; early onset = worse prognosis. ↑ rates in immigrants. African American patients ~5× and Latino ~3× more likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia/psychosis; Black patients with severe depression more often misdiagnosed as schizophrenia. Religious delusions more common in Christian societies; stigma affects outcome—Cultural bias → over-diagnosis; cultural awareness needed—⭐ Schizophrenia appears by early–mid 20s in males and late 20s in females; early onset = worse prognosis

Causes of schizophreniaChild of affected parent 10× risk; heritability ~80%; epigenetics (DNA methylation/acetylation). Environment: viruses (in-utero influenza), fetal malnutrition, obstetric complications, urban living, immigration, tobacco and cannabis, advanced paternal age, late winter/early spring birth, inflammatory disease (interstitial cystitis, celiac, thyrotoxicosis). ↑ dopamine in mesolimbic pathway (dopamine); also glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine. DTI: ↓ white-matter connectivity in prefrontal/temporal lobes—Antipsychotics aren't universally effective → not dopamine aloneD2-blocking antipsychotics⭐ Risk factors: cannabis/tobacco, urban living, immigration, paternal age, late-winter/early-spring birth; main NT = ↑ mesolimbic dopamine

COMPARE — Schizophrenia vs cluster A personality disordersSchizotypal: magical thinking (like delusions but less severe). Schizoid: withdrawal + blunted affect mimic negative symptoms (no desire for social interaction). Assessment & treatment principles — psychotic disordersEstablish safety and medical needs. Rule-out tests: thyroid function, ammonia (hepatic encephalopathy), urine copper (Wilson), vitamin B12, brain imaging. Clinical interview = primary tool; suicide risk assessment. Antipsychotics block mesolimbic dopamine → ↓ positive symptoms; FGA (haloperidol) more AEs than SGA (risperidone, olanzapine). Goal = consistency (IM depot q3–4 weeks)—Nonpharm: intensive outpatient + case management (adherence); family therapy ↓ relapseAntipsychotics for schizophrenia, schizoaffective, schizophreniform, brief psychotic⭐ Antipsychotics are the mainstay; family therapy decreases relapse in schizophrenia

Anxiety disorders — overview & DSM-5 classesNTs: serotonin, GABA, norepinephrine. DSM-5 split into 3 classes: Anxiety disorders · Obsessive-compulsive & related · Trauma- & stressor-related. Childhood-diagnosed: separation anxiety, selective mutism, RAD, DSED. Most treated with medication, CBT, or both; many start in childhood and persist; must cause distress/impairment; not due to substance or specific stressor; assess comorbid SUDTIMING matters (e.g., acute stress vs PTSD)Anxiety & depression = 2 most common problems in primary care; 1 in 5 primary-care patients has an anxiety disorderMedication ± CBT⭐ Social anxiety, panic disorder and GAD are the most common anxiety disorders in primary care

CBT & exposure therapy (concept)CBT = family of therapies: cognitive (change the thought → change the emotion) or behavioral (change the behavior). Model links thoughts, emotions, physical sensations, behaviors. Learning theories: classical conditioning (Pavlov, paired stimuli), operant conditioning (Skinner, consequences), social learning (Bandura, observation/modeling). Exposure therapy uses a graded fear hierarchy—Exposure + response prevention = OCD-specific formPhobias, social anxiety, panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD⭐ Exposure therapy works through a graded fear hierarchy

Social anxiety disorder (social phobia)Marked fear/avoidance of social situations involving scrutiny (conversation, being observed eating/drinking, performing). Fear of negative evaluation (humiliation, embarrassment, rejection); situation almost always provokes fear; avoided or endured; out of proportion> 6 monthsFear is of negative evaluation by othersCBT, systematic desensitization, SSRIs, β blockers. US annual 3–7%, lifetime 5–12%⭐ Social anxiety = fear of negative evaluation (scrutiny) for >6 months; SSRIs, β blockers, CBT

Panic attack (concept / specifier)Abrupt surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes with ≥ 4 of: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/hot flushes, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dyingPeaks within minutesOccurs with several disorders — panic attack alone ≠ panic disorderRule out medical causes⭐ A panic attack alone does not equal panic disorder

Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected panic attacks + ≥ 1 month of persistent worry about more attacks and/or maladaptive behavior change (avoiding unfamiliar places); not substance/medical≥ 1 month of worry/behavior changeAttacks are unexpected; anticipatory worry. Prevalence 2–3%, F:M 2:1, onset late adolescence/early adulthoodCBT, antidepressants. ↑ suicidality; comorbid substance use, depression, other anxiety⭐ Panic disorder = recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month of worry about further attacks

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)Obsessions: recurrent intrusive, unwanted thoughts/urges/images causing anxiety; person tries to suppress/neutralize. Compulsions: repetitive behaviors/mental acts driven by obsession or rigid rules, aimed at reducing anxiety. Themes: contamination → washing; symmetry → ordering/counting; taboo thoughts → praying; harm → checking. Check for insightTime consuming > 1 hour/day or distress/impairment; lifetime 2–3%; mean onset 19.5 yEgo-dystonic intrusive thoughts + neutralizing compulsionsCBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP); SSRIs (try ≥ 2), clomipramine (TCA), SNRI venlafaxine, SGAs; TMS; DBS for treatment-resistant⭐ OCD: >1 h/day of obsessions/compulsions; ERP + SSRIs (try at least two) or clomipramine

Somatic & dissociativeSomatic Symptom & Related Disorders (Somatic Symptoms and Dissociative Disorders) [Psychiatry · Behavioral Science]· 12FORMAT — one row per DSM-5-TR disorder (core criteria → duration/threshold → how to tell it apart → treatment); COMPARE rows contrast look-alikes; concept rows hold stand-alone teaching points

Physical symptom — sorting the somatic disorders

  1. Mild or no symptoms, fear of diseaseIllness anxiety disorder
  2. Symptom beyond medical explanation, unintentionalSomatic symptom disorder, FNSD (conversion) — or a 'masked' depressive/anxiety disorder
  3. Intentional, unconscious motivationFactitious disorder
  4. Intentional, conscious motivation (external gain)Malingering
Somatic Symptoms and Dissociative Disordersp.5Somatic Symptoms and Dissociative Disordersp.18
1 / 2
DisorderCore features / DSM-5-TR criteriaDuration · thresholdKey differentiatorTreatment⭐ Will Be TestedImage
Somatic symptom disorders — etiology (concept)Neurobiological: neuroendocrine dysfunction processing sensory/emotional info; misinterpreting normal sensations. Psychodynamic: conflict from childhood trauma/abuse — primary gain (unconsciously expressing/avoiding unacceptable emotion). Cognitive-behavioral: secondary gain (attention, care, avoiding responsibility); reinforcement of somatic expression. Sociocultural: culturally sanctioned expression of distress—Primary gain = unconscious internal; secondary gain = external benefit of symptoms—⭐ Primary gain = unconscious relief of internal conflict; secondary gain = attention, care, avoided responsibility
Somatic Symptoms and Dissociative Disorders
p.3
Somatic symptoms — diagnostic challenges (concept)Somatic symptoms = main reason people see doctors; 1 in 3 primary-care visits ends without a diagnosis. SSD can be diagnosed with known medical disease — look at the response TO it. Strong link with depression/anxiety. Many exams/procedures/surgeries → iatrogenic morbidity; costly; doctors often view patients negatively—Ethical dilemma: miss a medical cause vs harm by medicalizing—⭐ Somatic symptom disorder can coexist with a real medical disease — judge the response to it
Somatic Symptoms and Dissociative Disorders
p.4
Somatic symptom disorderA. ≥ 1 symptom significantly disrupting daily life. B. Excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors about it, ≥ 1 of: persistent thoughts about seriousness, persistent high anxiety, excessive time/energy. Specify: predominant pain; persistent. Severity: mild (1 B symptom), moderate (≥ 2), severe (≥ 2 + multiple complaints). Risk: female, less education, lower SES, alexithymia, childhood illness, abuse/traumaTypically > 6 months (< 6 mo = brief SSD)Symptoms present and real to patient — not intentional; focus is the symptom (vs IAD: the disease)Regular short-interval visits; therapeutic alliance; limit tests; educate on mind-body; CBT, mindfulness; health psychologist; specific antidepressants, St. John's wort. Screen: PHQ-15, SSS-8⭐ Somatic symptom disorder: ≥1 distressing symptom + excessive thoughts/anxiety/time for >6 months; treat with regular scheduled visits

Illness anxiety disorderPreoccupation with having or acquiring a serious disease; somatic symptoms mild or absent; high health anxiety; excessive health behaviors (body checking) or maladaptive avoidance (avoids doctors). Specify care-seeking vs care-avoiding type≥ 6 months (< 6 mo = brief IAD)Fear of the disease, not the symptom; tests negative and reassurance failsSame approach as SSD (alliance, limited testing, CBT)⭐ Illness anxiety: preoccupation with having a disease, symptoms mild/absent, ≥6 months

Functional neurological symptom disorder (FNSD, conversion)≥ 1 symptom of altered voluntary motor or sensory function, incompatible with neurological findings (internal inconsistency on retesting); not better explained; distress/impairment. Types: weakness/paralysis, abnormal movements, swallowing, speech, attacks/seizures, anesthesia, special senses, mixed. La belle indifference may or may not be present. ~5% of neurology referrals; F:M ≥ 2:1; childhood sexual abuse association; psychogenic (Freud: forbidden wish vs conscience)Often sudden onset after a stressorExam signs: Hoover's sign, tremor ↑ with weights, sharp-bordered glove anesthesia, blind but avoids obstacles, deaf but blinks to noise, seizures without injury/incontinence or AED response, paraplegia with normal reflexes/MEPsNot intentional; validate, rule out organic disease⭐ FNSD: neuro deficit incompatible with exam (Hoover's sign, inconsistent retest); la belle indifference optional

Factitious disorder imposed on selfFalsification of physical/psychological symptoms or induction of injury/disease; presents self as ill (sick role); deception evident without external rewards; not better explained. Red flags: inconsistencies, multiple providers, leaves AMA, many procedures, new symptoms after negative tests, detailed medical knowledge, eagerness for tests, enjoys hospitalization, reluctance to release recordsSpecify single or recurrent episodesIntentional production, unconscious motivation (need to be cared for); no external gainNot specified in lecture⭐ Factitious disorder: intentional symptoms with no external reward — motivation is the sick role

Factitious disorder imposed on another (formerly Munchausen by proxy)Falsification or induction of illness in another person (victim); presents victim as ill; no external rewards; not another mental disorder. Red flags: multiple/rare diagnoses, many specialists/procedures, abrupt severe symptoms; symptoms vanish when separated from caregiver (foster care)Specify single or recurrentPerpetrator gets the diagnosis, not the victimSeparate victim from perpetrator (child protective response)⭐ Imposed on another: caregiver fabricates the child's illness; symptoms resolve when the child is removed

MalingeringIntentional production of false or grossly exaggerated symptoms motivated by external incentives (avoid work/military duty, money, evade prosecution, obtain drugs). Suspect with medico-legal context (referred by attorney) or marked discrepancy between claimed disability and objective findings—Conscious motivation + external gain. Not a DSM-5-TR diagnosis (V code)—⭐ Malingering = conscious faking for external gain; a V code, not a DSM diagnosis

COMPARE — Somatic symptom vs illness anxiety vs FNSD vs factitious vs malingeringSSD: excessive thoughts/feelings about real symptoms. IAD: preoccupation with disease, symptoms mild/absent. FNSD: motor/sensory deficit incompatible with neuro findings. Factitious: deliberate falsification, no external reward. Malingering: intentional, external incentiveSSD & IAD ≥ 6 monthsProduction: unintentional (SSD, FNSD, IAD) vs intentional (factitious, malingering). Motivation: unconscious (factitious) vs conscious (malingering)—⭐ Intentional + unconscious motive = factitious; intentional + conscious external gain = malingering

Differential diagnosis — somatic symptom disordersMisdiagnosed physical illness: early connective tissue disease (SLE, RA); CNS disorders (tumor, MS, epilepsy, dementia, stroke, myasthenia gravis); endocrine (hypoglycemia, thyroid, porphyria). Chronic fatigue syndrome (fatigue > 6 months); fibromyalgia (widespread pain, tender points). Also depression, panic, GAD, IAD, FNSD, delusional, BDD, OCD, factitious, malingering—Physical illness can be comorbid—⭐ SLE, MS, myasthenia gravis and porphyria are classic medical mimics of somatic symptom disorders

Dissociative disorders — overviewSudden but temporary loss of memory or identity, or detachment from self/environment, with normal level of consciousness. Etiology: defense mechanisms of repression and dissociation after recent stressful event; early-life stressors esp. incest/childhood sexual abuse. Start in early adulthood, episodic, may last yearsEpisodicConsciousness normal—⭐ Dissociative disorders: memory/identity loss with normal consciousness, often after childhood sexual abuse

Dissociative amnesia (± dissociative fugue)Inability to recall important personal information (usually traumatic/stressful), inconsistent with ordinary forgetting; not substance/neurologic/medical; not another mental disorder. More common in young adults and women. Fugue: wandering/travel, may adopt a new identity, no memory of how they got there—Fugue = amnesia + purposeful travel/new identity—⭐ Dissociative fugue: travels away and adopts a new life with no memory of the old one

Personality traits & coping styles (concept)Traits = ways of coping/responding to relationships; on a continuum (low self-esteem → healthy → arrogance → narcissistic PD); shaped by genetic temperament + life experience; become a disorder when they cause distress or impair functioning. Coping with illness: withdrawn/suspicious (odd), emotional/seductive (dramatic), anxious, fearful, needy (avoidant/dependent)—Understanding traits helps predict responses and adherenceWithdrawn → take time to build trust; dramatic → set limits, closed-ended questions; anxious → address underlying concerns⭐ Emotional/seductive coping → set limits and use closed-ended questions
Personality Disordersp.3Personality Disordersp.4
1 / 2
COMPARE — Personality disorders vs other mental disordersOther disorders (MDD, anxiety) = autoplastic: problem within, ego-dystonic, episodic, varies with life events, elicit empathy, patient feels ill. PDs = alloplastic: problem projected out, ego-syntonic, stable and long-lasting, inflexible and pervasive, elicit strong countertransference, others feel illPD onset by adolescence/early adulthoodRemission on prior occasions → other disorder, not PDBoth: distress/impairment; rule out substance/medical⭐ PDs are ego-syntonic and stable; episodic, ego-dystonic symptoms suggest another disorder
Personality Disorders
p.5
Transference & countertransference (concept)Transference: patient's unconscious transfer of feelings/attitudes from a past person/situation onto the present (e.g., the doctor). Countertransference: feelings evoked in the doctor by the patient's transference—Countertransference is a useful guide to the patient's expectations; awareness allows reflection rather than unthinking reactionMonitor countertransference — esp. cluster B⭐ Countertransference = the doctor's feelings evoked by the patient's transference
Personality Disorders
p.6
General diagnostic criteria for personality disordersA. Enduring pattern deviating from cultural expectations in ≥ 2 of: cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, impulse control. B. Inflexible and pervasive. C. Distress/impairment. D. Stable, long duration. E. Not another mental disorder. F. Not substance/medicalOnset traceable to adolescence or early adulthoodPervasive across situations; stable—⭐ PD criterion A needs ≥2 of cognition, affectivity, interpersonal functioning, impulse control

Treatment approaches by clusterOften 'difficult' patients (indifferent, weird, suspicious, immoral, unstable, melodramatic, egotistical, fragile, submissive, controlling); needs a psychologically well physician. Cluster A: clear, consistent, non-defensive information; maximize control/autonomy; don't withhold information; don't argue. Cluster B: boundaries; firm, fair, consistent; monitor countertransference. Cluster C: avoid helplessness/hopelessness cycle; 'bear witness' without fixing; relaxation & complementary approaches—Cluster B = boundaries + monitor countertransferenceBorderline: DBT, transference-focused psychotherapy⭐ Cluster B patients need firm, fair, consistent boundaries

Substance useSubstance Use Disorders — Foundations & Frameworks (TBL: Substance Use Disorders, Parts 1 & 4) [Psychiatry & Behavioural Health · Psychiatry]· 7One row per SUD concept — col 2 = what it is / criteria, col 3 = numbers & thresholds, col 4 = exam differentiator, col 5 = what to do

Stages of change (transtheoretical model)

  1. PrecontemplationNo intention to stop; unaware the use is a problem (denial common)
  2. ContemplationStarting to recognize consequences; may foresee stopping
  3. PreparationPreparing to stop, usually within the next 30 days
  4. ActionActively taking steps to stop
  5. Maintenance & relapse preventionTypically abstinent ~6 months; relapse is an expected part of recovery

Substance use disorder (SUD) — DSM-5-TRPattern of use causing clinically significant impairment or distress; ≥2 of 11 criteria: larger amounts / longer than intended, persistent desire or failed attempts to cut down, much time obtaining/using/recovering, craving, failure of role obligations (work, school, home), use despite social/interpersonal problems, important activities given up, use in physically hazardous situations, use despite known physical/psychological harm, tolerance, withdrawal (relieved by more substance). 10 classes: alcohol, caffeine, cannabis, hallucinogens (PCP separate), inhalants, opioids, sedatives/hypnotics/anxiolytics, stimulants, tobacco, other/unknown≥2 criteria within 12 months. Severity: mild 2-3 · moderate 4-5 · severe ≥6. Early remission = no criteria >3 but <12 months; sustained remission = no criteria ≥12 months; 'in a controlled environment' if no access to the substanceDSM-5 merged 'abuse' and 'dependence' into one SUD with severity specifiers; 'drug addiction' is not a diagnostic term (uncertain definition, negative connotation). Antidepressants are NOT a DSM SUD classTailor to the individual and the substance (type, amount, frequency, route); psychosocial interventions most effective; multidisciplinary (GP, psychiatrist, social worker, community programs)⭐ SUD = ≥2 of 11 criteria within 12 months; mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe ≥6; sustained remission ≥12 months

SUD — epidemiology & risk factors~8% of people ≥12 y have a SUD (6% alcohol, 3% illicit drugs, 1% both); later national survey 14.5% (10.2% AUD, 6.6% illicit drug use disorder). ~80% of adolescents try alcohol, 50% an illicit drug. Highly heritable — a first-degree relative with addiction is one of the strongest predictors. Other risks: family dysfunction, negative life events, low self-esteem, poor social connections. Protective: social clubs, sports, higher education1 in 11 US ED visits due to illicit/non-medical drug use; 108,285 overdose deaths in the 12 months ending Dec 2023. Past-year use peaks at 18-25 y for every drug classAge at first use = strongest predictor of future/continued use (the developing frontal cortex is extra-sensitive to dopamine)Educate children & adolescents, screen for risk factors → early intervention⭐ The younger the age at first use, the higher the risk of a persisting use disorder

Brain reward pathway (mesocorticolimbic system)Ventral tegmental area → nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic) and VTA → prefrontal cortex (mesocortical); drugs release dopamine, strengthening the circuit and motivating repetition. Tolerance = attenuated euphoria → more drug for the same effect. Withdrawal = depleted DA stores + desensitized DA receptors (new homeostasis) → dysphoria, craving. Triggers: mood change, a specific person, withdrawalWithdrawal symptoms vary by substance: headache, N/V, abdominal pain, tremor, restlessness, insomnia, hyperphagia, seizures, hallucinations; alcohol withdrawal can start within hoursMRI: reduced grey matter in methamphetamine users and chronic AUD; functional imaging ↓ frontal-cortex activity. Distractors: nigrostriatal = motor/Parkinson, tuberoinfundibular = prolactin, corticospinal = motor, spinothalamic = pain/temperatureAdolescents: frontal cortex (impulse control, risk assessment) highly DA-sensitive → screen early; ask every admitted patient about alcohol⭐ SUD reward pathway = mesocorticolimbic (VTA, nucleus accumbens, frontal cortex), mainly dopamine

Key terms — tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, relapse, risk reductionDrug abuse: self-administration deviating from approved medical/social patterns. Misuse: inappropriate use. Compulsive use: continued despite adverse consequences. Addiction: overwhelming involvement with procuring/using. Tolerance: ↓ response with repeated dosing (cross-tolerance possible). Physical dependence: continued use needed to prevent withdrawal. Withdrawal: physical/psychological signs on abstinence. Abstinence: cessation. Relapse: renewed use after abstinenceRisk (harm) reduction: strategies that reduce medical/social harm and do NOT require abstinence (e.g., nicotine replacement, agonist substitution)Abstinence vs risk reduction = the two possible treatment goalsRelapse is an expected part of recovery → relapse-prevention focus in maintenance⭐ Physical dependence = continued use required to prevent withdrawal; risk reduction does not require abstinence

SUD screening & assessment toolsAdolescents only: S2BI (Screening to Brief Intervention) and BSTAD (Brief Screener for Tobacco, Alcohol and other Drugs). Adults: TAPS, NIDA Quick Screen / Modified ASSIST, AUDIT-C (self or clinician), AUDIT (clinician), Opioid Risk Tool (ORT, opioids), CAGE (alcohol), CAGE-AID (alcohol + other drugs). AUDIT-C: how often you drink · drinks on a typical day · how often ≥6 drinks on one occasionCAGE: Cut down? Annoyed by criticism? Guilty? Eye-opener in the morning? Single question: 'how often in the past year ≥4 (men) / ≥3 (women) drinks in a day?'S2BI and BSTAD are the only adolescent-specific tools; ORT is the opioid-specific toolPositive screen → detailed history, exam (signs of liver disease: jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly), labs incl. urine drug screen → diagnose with DSM-5 criteria⭐ Adolescent-only screens: S2BI and BSTAD; CAGE = Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener

SUD treatment principles — MI, stages of change, 12-step, smoking cessationMotivational interviewing: goal-oriented, patient-centred, explores ambivalence and readiness to change. Stages of change (transtheoretical): precontemplation → contemplation → preparation (within 30 days) → action → maintenance & relapse prevention. Alcoholics Anonymous 12 steps — one of the most effective routes to long-term sobrietyMI: 1-4 sessions of 15-45 min. Smoking: average 8-11 (up to 30) quit attempts; ~7 attempts before long-term abstinence; cravings persist for yearsDenial ('disease of denial') is often unconscious in precontemplation → use a confrontation statement ('It appears likely that alcohol is causing your health problems'), avoid judgmental/fear statements ('You must stop')Smoking: nicotine replacement (gum, patch) = first line; varenicline (partial α4β2 agonist); bupropion (NET/DAT inhibitor; can combine with NRT; avoid with seizure risk). E-cigarettes not recommended for cessation (AHA)⭐ Nicotine replacement therapy is first-line for smoking cessation; bupropion and varenicline are the other options

Substance useAlcohol-Related Disorders (TBL: Substance Use Disorders, Parts 2-4) [Psychiatry & Behavioural Health · Psychiatry]· 9One row per alcohol-related disorder — core features / DSM-5-TR criteria · duration / threshold / onset · key differentiator · treatment (Wernicke-Korsakoff → Delirium section)

Alcohol withdrawal timeline

  1. 4-12 hWithdrawal begins: tremor, anxiety, agitation, insomnia, N/V, autonomic hyperactivity (stage 1)
  2. Stages 2-4Visual/tactile hallucinations may appear if not treated
  3. Stage 3Generalized tonic-clonic seizures typically peak
  4. Day 2Symptoms peak
  5. Stage 4Delirium tremens in <10%: severe autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, confusion, hallucinations
  6. Days 4-5Dramatic improvement — episode usually lasts 4-5 days
  7. 3-6 monthsLow-level anxiety and insomnia may persist

Managing alcohol detox → maintenance

  1. AdmitHospitalization often needed for safe monitoring
  2. Fluids & electrolytesReplace K, Mg, phosphate
  3. Thiamine firstThiamine in ALL cases, before glucose (banana bag: thiamine, folate, multivitamin, 5% glucose, saline)
  4. BenzodiazepineDiazepam or chlordiazepoxide (or barbiturate) — cross-tolerant, prevents seizures; taper
  5. AvoidAntipsychotics (↑ seizures); β-blockers & clonidine (mask seizure warning signs)
  6. MaintenanceEducation, AA / SMART / Rational Recovery, psychotherapy, MI; naltrexone or acamprosate (1st), disulfiram (2nd)

Alcohol use disorder (AUD)Pervasive alcohol use affecting daily functioning; ≥2 of the 11 SUD criteria (more/longer than intended, can't cut down, craving, role failure e.g. skipping work for hangovers, use despite family problems, hazardous use e.g. drink-driving, tolerance, withdrawal…). Medical clues: withdrawal, injury/trauma, co-occurring anxiety/depression/other SUD, HTN, GI symptoms, ↑ liver enzymes, malnutrition (protein, folate, B6, thiamine). Causes: genetics up to 50% (adoptees follow biological parents), childhood conduct disorder & ADHD, extroversion/neuroticism/impulsivity, GABA-mimetic 'nanny neuron' calm, rapid onset, self-medication, drinking culture≥2 criteria in 12 months (mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe ≥6). 6.2% of US adults; men 12.4% vs women 4.9%; Native American 12.1%; 16.2% of 18-29 y, ~20% of college students. Peak onset early-mid 20s; course of remissions/relapses. Heavy drinking: men ≥14/week or ≥4/occasion; women ≥7/week or ≥3/occasionAUD = a pervasive pattern impairing function — distinct from acute intoxication or withdrawal (an AUD patient may present with either); assess daily intake. Binge drinking to unconsciousness is not normalPsychosocial: CBT, 12-step (AA, SMART Recovery, Rational Recovery), MI. Drugs: naltrexone (1st line; opioid antagonist ↓ craving; CI hepatitis/liver failure), acamprosate (1st line; weak NMDA antagonist/GABA-A; CI renal disease, pregnancy; OK in liver disease), disulfiram (2nd line; aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor → acetaldehyde reaction; 'hidden' alcohol in sauces, cough syrup)⭐ AUD: ≥2 criteria within 12 months, peak onset early-mid 20s; naltrexone & acamprosate first line, disulfiram second line

Alcohol intoxicationRecent ingestion + problematic behavioural/psychological change (mood, judgment, inappropriate behaviour) + ≥1 shortly after: slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impaired attention/memory (blackouts), stupor or coma. Not better explained by another disorder or substancePeak level within 30 min; zero-order elimination 7-10 g/h (0.5-1 drink/h). 1 standard drink = 0.6 fl oz (~13 g) pure alcohol = 12 oz beer 5% / 5 oz wine 12% / 1.5 oz liquor 40%. Rectal enema bypasses first-pass → rapid life-threatening levelsMechanism: GABA-A positive allosteric modulator (alcohol 'indirectly stimulates GABA receptors') + NMDA inhibition; ↑ dopamine & opioid peptides. Women reach higher levels (total body water). Habitual drinkers may be more intoxicated than exam suggests. Severe → respiratory depression, coma, death; contributes to suicide, violence, accidentsObservation, IV hydration; screen for AUD; brief intervention + referral (AA, clinic)⭐ Alcohol intoxication = slurred speech, unsteady gait, nystagmus, memory impairment; alcohol indirectly stimulates GABA receptors

Alcohol withdrawalAfter cessation of prolonged heavy use, ≥2 within hours-days: autonomic hyperactivity (↑HR, sweating, ↑BP), ↑ hand tremor, insomnia, nausea/vomiting, transient visual/tactile (or auditory) hallucinations, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Causes significant distress/impairment; not due to another condition or substanceBegins 4-12 h after last drink; peaks on day 2; dramatic improvement by days 4-5 (episode lasts 4-5 days); anxiety & insomnia may persist 3-6 months. Seizures typically peak in stage 3Chronic use ↑ glutamate (compensation); removing GABA inhibition leaves excess excitation. Life-threatening — monitor for seizures (not bradycardia, hyporeflexia or respiratory depression). Sedative/hypnotic withdrawal looks identical (up to 30% seizures). Post-op or post-admission agitation, tremor, 'bugs crawling' = withdrawalHospitalize; fluids & electrolytes (K, Mg, phosphate); thiamine in all cases (banana bag); benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide; taper) or barbiturates (cross-tolerant, treat/prevent seizures). Antipsychotics contraindicated (↑ seizure risk); β-blockers & clonidine not recommended (mask signs predicting a seizure)⭐ Alcohol withdrawal starts 4-12 h, peaks day 2, lasts 4-5 days; the life-threatening sign to watch is seizures; treat with benzodiazepines + thiamine

Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal delirium)Most severe form of withdrawal: severe autonomic hyperactivity (↑HR, sweating, ↑BP), marked tremor, confusion/disorientation, visual or auditory hallucinations<10% of people in withdrawal; stage 4 (after the stage-3 seizure peak)Delirium (impaired attention/orientation) on top of withdrawal; listed among alcohol-induced disorders as 'alcohol withdrawal delirium'Medical emergency — immediate attention: hospital monitoring, benzodiazepines, fluids/electrolytes, thiamine; no antipsychotics⭐ DTs affect <10% of withdrawals: severe autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, confusion, hallucinations — needs immediate care

Alcohol-induced mental disordersSymptoms severe enough to need independent clinical attention: alcohol-induced psychotic, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, sleep, sexual-dysfunction, and major/mild neurocognitive disorders; alcohol intoxication delirium; alcohol withdrawal deliriumTemporally linked to intoxication/withdrawal; usually resolve without treatment within days-weeks of stoppingLook identical to the primary disorder — the clue is the temporal relationship with alcohol; if symptoms persist outside alcohol use → an independent disorder needing different treatmentAbstinence, then reassess; treat any persisting independent disorder⭐ Alcohol-induced disorders mimic primary psychiatric disorders but track intoxication/withdrawal and resolve within days-weeks

Alcohol — metabolism & medical complicationsHepatocyte: alcohol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid using NAD+ → ↑ NADH/NAD+ → lactic acidosis + acetyl-CoA → triglycerides → reversible fatty liver → cirrhosis → portal HTN, ascites, varices, ↑ NH3 (brain). Also acute hepatitis, gastritis, pancreatitis; malnutrition (folate, thiamine), hyponatremia; permanent cognitive impairment, Wernicke-Korsakoff, incoordination, peripheral neuropathy; aspiration pneumonia (Klebsiella, anaerobes); SCC of mouth/larynx/esophagus, HCC, breast cancer90% hepatic, zero-order; >100 mg/dL induces CYP2E1 → faster metabolism of acetaminophen (→ toxic NAPQI), phenytoin, warfarin, propranolol, benzodiazepines. Tolerance to intoxication but only a minor rise in lethal dose. >75% of US adults drink; ~95,000 alcohol deaths/yrToxic alcohols used when beverages unavailable: isopropyl (rubbing alcohol), methanol ('moonshine'), ethylene glycol (antifreeze); alcohol hidden in mouthwash/cough syrupAbstinence; nutrition & thiamine/folate; examine for liver disease⭐ Alcohol oxidation ↑ NADH/NAD+ → lactic acidosis & fatty liver; chronic heavy use induces CYP2E1 (acetaminophen → NAPQI)

Opioids (heroin, fentanyl, carfentanil, prescription)Euphoria, depressed mental status, miosis, respiratory depression, constipation, bradycardiaFlu-like: N/V, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, muscle aches, fever, sweating, chills, rhinorrhea, agitation, anxiety, tachycardia, HTN. Exam: dilated pupils, yawning, piloerection, lacrimation, hyperactive bowel sounds. Rarely fatal but almost unbearable (negative reinforcement)Fentanyl now leads overdose deaths (in heroin since 2013; lethal ~2 mg); carfentanil ~10,000× morphine, 100× fentanyl (elephant tranquilizer; danger to first responders). Tolerance up to 100× usual doseOverdose: naloxone (IV/IM/intranasal; may precipitate withdrawal). OUD: methadone (full μ agonist, long t½, specialty clinic; resp. depression), buprenorphine (partial μ agonist — ceiling ↓ overdose; SL/SC; precipitates withdrawal with full agonist), naltrexone (μ antagonist; only after 1 week opioid-free; poor compliance)⭐ Opioid intoxication = miosis + respiratory depression (reverse with naloxone); withdrawal = dilated pupils, yawning, piloerection, diarrhea — miserable but rarely fatal

CocaineEuphoria, agitation/psychosis, chest pain, seizures, tachycardia/HTN, mydriasis; intoxication <1 h'Crash': ↑ appetite, hypersomnia, intense psychomotor retardation, severe depression; no significant exam findingsBlocks DAT (reward/abuse), NET (HTN, tachycardia) and SERT + voltage-gated Na+ channels (historic local anesthetic). Short t½ (~1 h) → repeated doses per occasion. ~2% US use (2020); ~1 in 5 overdose deaths. Chronic: paranoia/psychosis indistinguishable from schizophrenia; sympathetic signs may be absent in chronic usersNo consistently effective pharmacotherapy for stimulant use disorder (DA agonists, bupropion, long-acting amphetamine tried)⭐ Cocaine blocks DA/NE/5-HT reuptake and Na+ channels; intoxication <1 h with mydriasis, chest pain, HTN

Cannabis (marijuana, THC)↑ appetite, euphoria, dysphoria/panic, slow reflexes, impaired time perception, dry mouth, conjunctival reddening; no respiratory depressionIrritability, anxiety, depressed mood, insomnia, ↓ appetite; no significant exam findings. Low dose ≈ acute confusional state; high dose → serious neurologic, CV and psychotic reactionsNo clear withdrawal syndromeNon-competitive NMDA antagonists; ketamine causes less agitation/psychiatric effects than PCP; acute or chronic use → long-lasting schizophrenia-like psychosisSupportive; protect from injury⭐ PCP = NMDA antagonist: violence + vertical/horizontal nystagmus + analgesia
