Deadly with alcohol or opioids (alcohol-benzodiazepine synergy → slowed breathing, ↓ O2 sat); used to self-medicate withdrawal from cocaine, opioids, alcoholSevere use disorder: switch to diazepam (long t½) then taper slowly over months⭐ Benzodiazepine withdrawal, like alcohol, can cause fatal seizures — switch to diazepam and taper over months

COMPARE — opioid vs stimulant intoxication & withdrawalOpioid: miosis, respiratory depression, bradycardia, constipation, depressed mental status. Cocaine/meth: mydriasis, tachycardia/HTN, chest pain, seizures, agitation/psychosisOpioid: dilated pupils, yawning, piloerection, lacrimation, diarrhea, hyperactive bowel sounds. Stimulant: crash — hypersomnia, ↑ appetite, psychomotor retardation, severe depression, no exam findingsPupils and bowel flip between intoxication and withdrawal; opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely fatalOpioid overdose → naloxone; stimulant → supportive (no effective drug)⭐ Small pupils + slow breathing = opioid; big pupils + HTN/chest pain = stimulant

Stimulants, nicotine, cannabis: psychological (dysphoria, appetite change), no significant physical findings. Disorder / substanceCore features / DSM-5-TR criteriaDuration · threshold · onsetKey differentiatorTreatment / management⭐ Will Be TestedImage
Intellectual disability (ID)Deficits in BOTH intellectual functioning (learning, problem-solving, judgment — confirmed by clinical assessment + standardized IQ testing) AND adaptive functioning in social, conceptual (reading, writing, math, memory) and practical (ADLs, money, technology) domains → limits ≥1 area of daily living without support. Severity mild/moderate/severe graded by adaptive functioning. 'Mental retardation' no longer usedOnset in developmental period. ~1% of US (more in boys); severe ~6/1000; mild ≫ severe. Course nonprogressive (plateau; may improve with intervention) — exception Rett (regression)vs major/mild NCD (loss of function); vs communication/learning disorders (no adaptive + intellectual deficit); vs ASD (deficits cluster in social communication). Causes: genetic >50% (trisomy 21, DiGeorge, Angelman, Prader-Willi, fragile X, Turner, Rett), TORCH, fetal alcohol, perinatal trauma/anoxia/hyperbilirubinemia, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, toxins. ↑ mental disorders & suicide; ASD often comorbidHistory (prenatal → postnatal, 3-generation family), physical exam ± genetic testing; hearing & vision tests first; standardized testing; psychoeducational + behavioural interventions, IEP (re-evaluated yearly), multidisciplinary team; drugs only for comorbid ADHD⭐ ID requires deficits in BOTH adaptive and intellectual functioning; it is nonprogressive (Rett is the exception)

Dyslexia = reading (accuracy, rate, comprehension); dyscalculia = math≥1 symptom for ≥6 months despite targeted intervention; onset in elementary school years; ~10% overall (US 5-15%), more in boys; family history ↑ risk 4-8× (reading), 5-10× (math); lifelongPresent since learning began — not new after head injury or new inattention. NeurodevelopmentalADHD & Autism Spectrum Disorder (Workshop: Neurodevelopmental Disorders / Stimulant Pharmacology, Parts 2-3) [Neurocognitive, Neurodegenerative & Development · Psychiatry]· 4One row per DSM-5-TR disorder — core features · duration / threshold / onset · key differentiator · treatment

ADHD — choosing the drug

  1. BaselineHeight, weight, BP, HR, tics, appetite, sleep, headaches/abdominal pain, substance use
  2. First line: stimulantAmphetamines (release DA/NE) or methylphenidate (DAT > NET blocker); IR in <6 y, long-acting for older children; drug holidays allowed; AEs appetite/growth suppression, ↑HR/BP, insomnia, tics
  3. Tics, anxiety, substance-abuse history, short statureAtomoxetine (NET inhibitor; no abuse potential; 1-4 wk onset, 6-12 wk full; no holidays; black box suicidal ideation; CYP2D6)
  4. Comorbid depressionBupropion (NET/DAT; ↑ seizure risk)
  5. Tics or can't tolerate higher stimulant doseGuanfacine/clonidine (α2A; taper to avoid rebound HTN; avoid in orthostatic hypotension)
  6. Obese child with orthostatic hypotensionMethylphenidate (appetite suppression; α2 agonists worsen hypotension)

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)Persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity interfering with functioning; subtypes: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Inattention: careless mistakes, can't sustain focus, doesn't listen, no follow-through, disorganized, avoids sustained mental effort, loses things, distractible, forgetful. Hyperactivity-impulsivity: fidgets, leaves seat, runs/climbs, can't play quietly, 'driven by a motor', talks excessively, blurts out answers, can't wait turn, interrupts≥6 symptoms (≥5 if ≥17 y) for ≥6 months; several symptoms before age 12; in ≥2 settings. Diagnosable from 3 y, usually by 12; M:F 4:1 (boys dx ~7 y, girls ~12 y); ~5% children, 2.5% adults; persists in up to 50%Inattentive ↔ ↓ norepinephrine; hyperactive-impulsive ↔ dopamine/serotonin. Genes DAT1/SLC6A2, DRD4, DRD5, 5HTTLPR; heritability 75-90% (relative affected 25-35%). Env: prenatal nicotine/alcohol, lead, low birth weight, family conflict. Imaging: ↓ grey matter, delayed cortical maturation. Ddx: sleep disorder (rule out first), mood disorder, lead. Comorbid: learning disorders, ODD (ADHD + ODD → 3× CD), CD (46%), anxiety; 60-80% of Tourette patients have ADHDParent + teacher rating scales (Vanderbilt, Conners, BASC, Barkley, Vineland); behavioural interventions, IEP. Stimulants 1st line (70-80% improve): amphetamines, methylphenidate. Non-stimulants: atomoxetine, bupropion, guanfacine/clonidine. Baseline height, weight, BP, HR, tics before starting⭐ ADHD: ≥6 symptoms (≥5 if ≥17 y) for ≥6 months, several before 12, in ≥2 settings; rule out sleep disorder; stimulants first line

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)Persistent deficits in social communication & interaction across settings (back-and-forth conversation, sharing emotions, slow response to name, ↓ eye contact/facial expression, relationships & imaginative play; high-pitched, robotic or sing-song voice) PLUS ≥2 restricted, repetitive behaviours: repetitive movements/speech/object use, insistence on sameness/rigid routines, fixated intense interests, sensory hyper/hyporeactivity. Specify ± ID, language impairment, genetic/medical conditionEarly developmental period; usually recognized 12-24 months (may emerge 6-12 mo); reliable diagnosis at ~2 y. 1 in 59 US children by age 8; boys 4× (1 in 37 vs 1 in 151); 1-2% worldwide (Hong Kong highest). Screen at 18 & 24 monthsRed flag: rapid loss of social/language skills in first 2 years. Merges autism, Asperger, childhood disintegrative disorder, PDD. Fragile X (FMR1) = most common single-gene cause (15% have a known mutation; also Down, Rett, tuberous sclerosis). ↓ GABA, ↓ glutamate, ↑ serotonin; accelerated brain growth 2-4 y, ↑ frontal gyrification. Env: prenatal insults, advanced parental age, low birth weight. Ddx: SCD (no RRBs), GDD/ID, giftedness, Landau-Kleffner, Rett, hearing loss, ADHD, anxiety, OCDM-CHAT-R/F screen (parents) → ADOS diagnosis (specialist; four 30-min modules); hearing & vision first; seizures → EEG, genetic & metabolic tests, imaging. No cure — start early: ABA (DTT, EIBI for <5 y, PRT, VBI), DIR/Floortime, TEACCH, OT, sensory integration, speech therapy, PECS. Drugs for symptoms: stimulants, α2 agonists, atomoxetine, risperidone, valproate, SSRIs (black-box suicidality). Poor prognosis: IQ <70, no joint attention by 4, no functional speech by 5, seizures⭐ ASD = social-communication deficits + ≥2 restricted/repetitive behaviours from early childhood; fragile X is the commonest single-gene cause

Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD)Severe recurrent temper outbursts (verbal/physical) grossly out of proportion and inconsistent with developmental level + persistently irritable/angry mood between outbursts most of the day, nearly every dayOutbursts ≥3×/week; ≥12 months (no symptom-free period >3 months); ≥2 settings (home, school, peers); onset before 10; cannot first be diagnosed before 6 or after 18; much more common in malesA depressive disorder (DSM-5) created to curb overdiagnosis of pediatric bipolar disorder. Cannot coexist with ODD — if criteria for both are met, diagnose DMDD (more severe). vs IED: IED is not irritable between outburstsCBT ± medication for symptoms⭐ DMDD = chronic irritability between ≥3 outbursts/week for ≥12 months; first diagnosed only between 6 and 18; trumps ODD

Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD)Angry/irritable, argumentative/defiant, vindictive pattern — ≥4 of: often loses temper, touchy/easily annoyed, angry & resentful, argues with authority figures/adults, actively defies rules/requests, deliberately annoys others, blames others for own mistakes, spiteful/vindictive ≥2× in 6 months≥4 symptoms for ≥6 months, shown with ≥1 person who is not a sibling. Lifetime 11% males, 9% females (1-16% of adolescents); consistent across cultures; symptoms often resolve by adulthoodDefies authority figures/rules but not societal norms — no law-breaking, normal friendships. Most common reason for child mental-health referral. Inconsistent discipline, neglect, abuse, poor frustration tolerance; ↓ serotonin activity. >90% later get another mental disorder; ADHD & anxiety comorbidParent management training = most effective (consistent, predictable consequences; less harsh punishment); PCIT, individual/family therapy, problem-solving & social-skills training. No medication for ODD itself (treat comorbid ADHD/anxiety)⭐ ODD: defiant/vindictive toward authority for ≥6 months without violating societal norms; parent management training is the best treatment

Intermittent explosive disorder (IED)Recurrent brief, unplanned impulsive verbal or physical aggressive outbursts out of proportion to provocation; no intent to harm or gain; patient distressed/guilty afterwards; not aggressive/irritable between outburstsAge ≥6 years; EITHER verbal/physical aggression without damage on average twice weekly for 3 months OR 3 damaging/injuring assaults in 12 months. 1-5% worldwide; median onset 14 y (late childhood/adolescence), often continues into adulthood; male↑ amygdala activity, ↓ grey matter, genetic link, abuse/neglect/witnessed violence; ↓ serotonin. >80% have another psychiatric disorder: MDD 37% (most common), AUD 33%, ODD 25%, CD 24%, ADHD 20%. Exclude head trauma, dementia, substanceCBT + medication: SSRI (fluoxetine) first line; 2nd line phenytoin or oxcarbazepine; then lamotrigine, topiramate, lithium, valproate⭐ IED: brief unplanned outbursts followed by guilt; serotonin deficit; fluoxetine first line; MDD the commonest comorbidity

Conduct disorder (CD)Repetitive pattern violating the rights of others and societal norms — ≥3 of 15: aggression to people/animals (bullying, fights, weapon, cruelty to people or animals, forced sex, mugging), property destruction (fire-setting, vandalism), deceit/theft (break-ins, lying, shoplifting), serious rule violation (out at night <13 y, running away, truancy <13 y). Planned, intentional, no remorse≥3 criteria in past 12 months; diagnosed <18 y; 6-16% boys, 2-9% girls. ~40% of boys / 20% of girls later → antisocial personality disorder (≥18 y)vs ODD: breaks laws/social norms, not just defies authority. vs IED: planned and remorseless. Risks: physical abuse, maternal smoking in pregnancy, family history, low parental involvement; ↓ serotonin. Comorbid ADHD (CD in 46% of ADHD), anxietyPCIT, family/individual therapy, cognitive problem-solving & social-skills training; no specific medication (treat comorbid ADHD/anxiety)⭐ Conduct disorder: ≥3 rights-violating behaviours (bullying, theft, fire-setting, cruelty) in 12 months, <18 y, no remorse; becomes antisocial PD at 18

EnuresisRepeated voiding of urine into bed or clothes (involuntary or intentional); during sleep, while awake, or both. Primary (never continent) vs secondary (continent, then lost — e.g., after a stressor). Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis = night-time only, no other urinary symptoms≥2×/week for ≥3 consecutive months (or significant distress); developmental age >5 years. 16% at 5 y → 7% at 8 y → 1-2% after 15 y; boys 2× (daytime enuresis more in girls); more common in black children (US)Causes: overactive detrusor, small bladder, ↑ nocturnal urine / low or ineffective ADH, disturbed sleep, genetics (parent affected → 50-75% vs 15%; father 10×, mother 4×), developmental delay, psychosocial stress; ↓ NE/DA. Exclude DM, DI, UTI (dysuria → urinalysis), neurogenic bladder (spina bifida), hypothyroidism, diuretics/lithium, pinworm, OSA, CKD. Associated ADHDBehavioural first: limit evening fluids, void before bed, night waking, child helps clean up, stop teasing, star charts (positive > negative motivation); enuresis alarm; then desmopressin (ADH analog; dilutional hyponatremia; good for sleepovers); imipramine (TCA, 3rd line — QT prolongation). Punishment doesn't help⭐ Enuresis: ≥2×/week for ≥3 months after age 5, medical causes excluded; behavioural/alarm first, then desmopressin

EncopresisRepeated passage of feces into inappropriate places (clothes, floor), involuntary or intentional; primary or secondary≥1×/month for ≥3 months; developmental age >4 years. 4% of 4-17 y; non-constipation type 4× more in boys; mostly resolved by adulthoodConstipation in 80% → stool-withholding → overflow incontinence (chronic constipation can cause 'diarrhea'); triggers: cow's milk, solids, toilet training, starting school, separation, drugs (TCAs, iron); other 20% psychosocial (abuse, eating disorders, regression); ↓ serotonin → ↓ motility. Constipation is the ONLY medical cause allowed. Ddx: cerebral palsy, hypotonia, ID, spina bifida, ectopic anus. Associated ADHD, ASDHistory & exam (abdominal palpation, DRE), abdominal x-ray (stool burden), psychosocial assessment, urinalysis; diet (prune/apple/pear juice 120-180 mL/day, avoid dairy, offer fibre), toilet sitting ~10 min after meals with foot support + praise; school nurse/teachers involved⭐ Encopresis: ≥1×/month for ≥3 months after age 4; constipation (80%) is the only medical cause that still permits the diagnosis

Disorder / substanceCore features / DSM-5-TR criteriaDuration · threshold · onsetKey differentiatorTreatment / management⭐ Will Be TestedImage
Tourette syndrome (Tourette disorder)Multiple motor tics + ≥1 vocal tic at some time (not necessarily together). Tics = sudden, rapid, recurrent involuntary movements/sounds; simple (eye blink, grunt) or complex (copropraxia, echopraxia, coprolalia, echolalia); premonitory urge relieved by the tic; worse when ill, tired, stressed, excited; can occur in sleep; can be partly suppressedTics persist >1 year since first tic; onset before 18. Tics in ~20% of school-age children, onset 4-6 y, peak 10-12 y, decline in adolescence; M:F 4:1; TS 1 in 360 (0.3%; maybe 0.6%); ~1% of adults persistMost severe tic disorder. SLITRK1 mutations; basal ganglia/frontal cortex; DA, 5-HT, NE abnormalities; ↓ left frontal grey matter. Risks: obstetric complications, older father, low birth weight, maternal smoking (modifiable). Most common ddx: transient tics of childhood; exclude substances (cocaine), epilepsy (temporal lobe), Huntington, CJD, encephalitis, stroke, head injury. Comorbid ADHD (60-80% of TS; usually diagnosed first), OCD, anxiety, LD, depressionOften none — educate & monitor. If impairing: CBT / habit reversal therapy first line; mild-moderate → clonidine/guanfacine; moderate-severe → risperidone or haloperidol (pimozide, aripiprazole — more AEs). Treat comorbid ADHD/OCD⭐ Tourette: multiple motor + ≥1 vocal tic for >1 year, onset <18; CBT/habit reversal first, then α2 agonists

MedulloblastomaMalignant pediatric cerebellar tumor; arises in the vermis / cerebellar peduncles around the 4th ventricle.Often WNT or SHH pathway mutations.Soft gray cerebellar mass. Small blue round cells, Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes; lumen = tangle of primitive neurites).Child, cerebellum, truncal ataxia, drop metastases via CSF. EpendymomaArises from the ependymal lining; children often 4th ventricle; adults spinal canal.NF2 association (deletion on chr 22), especially spinal forms.Ventricular mass causing hydrocephalus; well circumscribed, solid or cystic with papillae. Perivascular pseudorosettes (lumen = blood vessel), true ependymal rosettes (clear lumen).4th ventricle, obstructive hydrocephalus, destruction of periventricular tissue, NF2. Matches the lecture.⭐ Perivascular pseudorosettes; 4th ventricle in children, spinal in adults/NF2.

MeningiomaMost common benign CNS tumor; attached to the meninges, often along the sagittal sinus; extra-axial nodules compressing adjacent tissue without invasion.NF2 mutation (chr 22).Well-circumscribed dural-based mass. Whorls, psammoma bodies, spindle-shaped cells.Elderly woman, parasagittal, dural tail, estrogen/progesterone/androgen receptors, common cause of epilepsy. The summary adds 'elderly woman' and dural tail; the lecture calls it the most common CNS tumor in adults (F:M 3:2).⭐ Dural-based, whorls + psammoma bodies, NF2, hormone receptors.

Primary CNS lymphoma (DLBCL)Usually in immunocompromised patients; EBV-associated in AIDS; deep white matter.Various B-cell mutations; PDL1 gene mutation.Periventricular infiltrative lesions, often multiple, well-circumscribed nodules. Large atypical lymphocytes around vessels (angiocentric pattern), CD19/CD20+.AIDS, EBV, ring-enhancing lesions, responds to steroids. The summary adds ring enhancement and steroid response; the lecture also covers immunocompetent young and middle-aged adults (PDL1, 45% 5-year survival).⭐ Angiocentric CD20+ B cells, deep/periventricular, EBV in AIDS.
